#4979. 11 Best Edinburgh Hotels for High-End Hospitality (2026)

Edinburgh’s hotel scene has been a slow burn. Long-standing staples have secured the Scottish capital’s place on the hospitality map, setting a tone that’s both old-world and wonderfully warm. These classic stays have always matched the Scottish capital’s more measured, thoughtful rhythm—grand yet accessible, historic but deeply hospitable. Recently, a new wave of openings and renovations has joined them, in step with Scotland’s creative pull. Chefs, makers, and artists have been moving in, opening craft bakeries, destination restaurants, and shop-meets-galleries in fast-rising neighborhoods—and the hotels, well, they’re responding. From colorful long-stay apartments to charming design boltholes and fancy grand dames, it’s easy to find an overnight stay that matches your aspirations.

If you’re in town for the Fringe and Hogmanay festivals, or en route to the Highlands, we’ve curated a list of prime spots throughout Edinburgh—from the New Town, Old Town, and even over to waterside Leith—that feel just as charming as the city itself.

Perks: Irene Forte spa, indoor lap pool, three on-site restaurants, whisky tasting experience, afternoon tea, concierge, views of Edinburgh landmarks, close proximity to Edinburgh Waverley Station

The Balmoral is one of the most popular stays and landmarks in Edinburgh. Its 190-foot clock tower—famously set three minutes fast, except on New Year’s Eve—has been part of the capital city's skyline since opening as a railway hotel in the early 1900s. After a multi-million-pound restoration by the Rocco Forte group was completed in 2025, much of the property’s charm remains in classic stained glass and the grand staircase. In true Olga Polizzi style, the interiors are a layered mix: milky creams, Hebridean blues, custom Balmoral tartan, and heather hues fill the property’s suites and communal spaces.

“The Balmoral does rest and relaxation like no other through comforting amenities, charming interiors, and hearty cuisine,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “After a long day of taking in Edinburgh’s historic sights, there was nothing I looked forward to more than the treats from turndown service and a long soak in the glossy marble tub.” Guests also return for the sprawling bedrooms, some of which frame picturesque views of Edinburgh Castle. All suites showcase cozy design with contemporary wallpaper prints, surprisingly neutral plaid furniture, and ultrasoft wool bed covers. Exceptional old-school services like shoe shining, unpacking, and proper concierge know-how are added perks, as is the on-site Irena Forte spa. “My masseuse was able to release all the tension I was holding in my upper back, which was no small feat,” Lee remarks. Afternoon tea is also a popular attraction—even if it skews English—along with whiskey tastings and golf excursions. From $399 per night.

Perks: Rooftop, close to Waverley train station, wellness studio

Fans of Gleneagles were thrilled when the storied countryside brand brought its rural Perthshire charm to the city in 2022. That same meticulous attention to detail has been carried into this glossy, members-club-meets-hotel in St Andrew’s Square. Don’t be deterred by the exclusive concept—non-members are welcome to stay and dine at the all-day restaurant, The Spence. Rooms are colorful and elegant, wrapped in soft pastels and plush velvets, while shared spaces include Lamplighters, a rooftop bar with knockout views, and a stylish wellness studio offering up fitness classes to an active audience. Like its big sister, service is warm and personal: Expect front desk staff who greet you by name and offer thoughtful local recs. From $805 per night.

Perks: Whole house takeover, private parking, 17th-century merchant’s house, fully equipped kitchen

Leith has quietly become one of Edinburgh’s most desirable neighborhoods—edgy, creative, and increasingly on the radar of out-of-town travelers looking for a longer stay. Tucked just off the Firth of Forth, The Pavilion at Lamb’s House is a rare find: a three-bedroom private home designed by architect couple Nick Groves-Raines and Kristín Hannesdóttir. Inspired by early 18th-century garden pavilions, it sits on the grounds of a restored 17th-century merchant’s house and offers a distinct sense of place. Interiors feel plucked from another time period—freestanding cast iron tubs, brown antique furniture, Victorian brass bed frames—and still manage to be quietly current. The sweet yellow box bedroom is a hit with kids, and grown-ups will appreciate the calm, thoughtful set up. A place to properly settle in and live like a (very lucky) local. From $642 per night for the whole property.

Perks: Georgian-influenced architecture, near Haymarket station, screening room

This property is a Scottish debut for the Hoxton (the hospitality group known for its open-house, community-driven hotels around the world) and was a hotly anticipated opening when it opened its doors this summer. 214 rooms are carefully spread out across 11 Georgian-style townhouses in Edinburgh’s Haymarket. Like its sister properties, punchy decor from Ennismore’s in-house AIME Studios blends the building’s heritage—curled cornicing and sash windows with splashes of color, including deep raspberry red headboards and playful pineapple coat hooks. Downstairs, the restaurant Patatino is set to become a quick hit for its classic Italian trattoria menu with a Scottish twist (including a sourdough pizza topped with ‘nduja, haggis, hot honey, and fior di latte). In theme with the brand, the lobby is also a laptop-toting, coffee-to-cocktails all day scene. Families can also peacefully put their kids to bed in the bunk rooms upstairs before spending an evening with a film in the five-seater screening room. From $203 per night.

Perks: Private, in the Grassmarket neighbourhood, architecturally striking

Perks: Steps from Waverly Station, top floor bar, central location

There’s a balanced mix of Scandi and Scottish style at this sleek stay just across from Waverley Station, Edinburgh’s main transport hub. The central location is a win for rail travelers who can wheel their luggage straight from the platform to check-in, and as Design Hotels’ first Scottish property, there’s real aesthetic appeal. Ditching the traditional lobby, arrival happens on the seventh floor, where panoramic views set the scene and a warm team offers tips on where to head next. Rooms are simple and contemporary, with nods to old-school Scotland via tartan touches, wooden floors, and a façade of locally sourced stone. The rooftop bar is a draw in its own right, with a far-reaching backdrop across to The Balmoral’s clock tower and the shifting lines of Edinburgh’s Old and New Towns. From $217 per night.

Perks: Self-catered studio apartments with individual kitchens, all-day café, coworking space

Perks: Views of Edinburgh Castle, near the centre of town, three restaurants

Taking over the historic India Buildings on Victoria Street, Virgin Hotels Edinburgh has brought a fresh, self-assured energy to the Old Town since its opening in 2022. The design walks a clever line between old and new—original stonework and ornate plaster ceilings are set off by bold color, rich textures, and a few playful surprises. Rooms, dubbed “chambers,” are smartly divided into dressing and sleeping zones with sliding doors, well-stocked SMEG fridges, and sharp detailing that feels considered and comforting. At its heart, this is a social hotel: The Commons Club is busy from brunch through to late-night cocktails, while Eve leans into the brand’s signature after-dark spirit. It’s a confident, well-executed arrival that feels right at home in Edinburgh. From $407 per night.

Perks: Cocktail bars, 24-hour service, 10-minute walk from Edinburgh Castle

Perks: Kitchen, washer and dryer, crib and baby accessories, security system, pet-friendly

It’s all about convenience at 33 Castle Terrace, which resembles a serviced apartment instead of a traditional hotel stay. Suites are equipped with a washer and dryer, meaning you’ll never have to worry about running out of clean clothes. The fully-equipped kitchen can help fulfill all of your culinary cravings. The interiors take inspiration from Scandinavian design, with neutral hues, clean-lined furniture, and thoughtful color layered in. It is a five-minute walk away from Edinburgh Castle, keeping you centrally located in Old Town near lots of shopping and some of the city’s best restaurants, like The Makar’s Mash Bar and The Piper’s Rest. From $243 per night.

Perks: Private balcony (select suites), kitchenette, rainfall shower, coffee maker, luggage drop-off allowed

Housed in a historic building dating back to 1875, splashy upgrades like marble-wrapped bathrooms, modern kitchen appliances, and colorful wall makeovers breathe new life into this aparthotel in New Town. For a welcoming feel, the property features cozy design elements like upholstered headboards, warm light fixtures, and classic furniture silhouettes. Fun fact: This stay also reflects Edinburgh’s architectural heritage with details like sandstone facade, arcaded ground floor, and mansard roofing since it formerly served as a storage space for the National Museum of Scotland. Other perks include direct access to the private Queen Street Gardens (typically reserved for residents) and close proximity to the Scottish National Portrait Gallery. From $240 per night.

Craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.

#4977. Reigning Champ Hellen Obiri Didn’t Change Much About This Year’s Prep for the NYC Marathon

Her secret weapon to a successful training block? A lot of naps and even more tea.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Speaking from personal experience, the closer you get to marathon day, the louder the worries become. Can I really make it to the start line when I’m so sore and tired all the time? Are my long runs and weekly mileage on par with everyone else’s? Do I even want to be doing this anymore? That is, unless you’re the reigning champion, Hellen Obiri.

This weekend, she’ll be making her return to the New York City Marathon—which she won last year in a course record of 2 hours, 19 minutes, 51 seconds. When I chatted with the On athlete a few weeks out from the race, she had just wrapped up a morning session of 12.4 miles and still had another five on deck later that day. It seems like a lot, but “the evening session is always very easy,” she assured me.

Obiri, 36, has won four marathons (NYC and Boston, two times each), and though she knows everyone will be watching to see if she’ll do it again, she doesn’t seem affected by the pressure. “When you're the reigning champion, everybody's looking at you and wondering what you can do,” she says. “You have that pressure of, ‘How can I win back to back?’”

But Obiri knows that in a marathon, anything can happen. It’s a long distance, and she’s competing against the best of the best—so she’s not counting a single person out. “For me, [the key] is to keep training well, and to keep that in my mind: I'm the defending champion,” Obiri says. “The most important thing is to stay safe and to stay healthy, and then everything's possible.”

Here’s what she’s doing to prepare for race day—and her advice to those heading to a starting line soon.

Because, well, it worked so well in 2025. “Sometimes we do study who is in the race,” she admits, though she didn’t name drop any one contender she has her eye on this year.

Each week, she logs over 100 miles, and gives herself two to three days to recover after a long run or speed session. (Recovery days still often consist of easy miles, though.) Her longest run heading into November 1? Twenty-four miles. Even the best of the best don’t run the full distance until race day.

She also preps—both physically and mentally—for pushing through particularly hard moments. Will she still have enough in the tank to keep pushing the pace with her speedy competitors come mile 20? What about in those last 100 meters if she needs to dig deep for a sprint finish?

It’s her second year working with On Athletic Club coach Laura Thweatt, who also boasts an impressive history with the NYC Marathon, placing eighth in 2021. Having a coach who has also raced New York has made a huge difference, Obiri says, because she knows what it’s like to train for this specific race and also what it takes to do well. Plus, Thweatt is able to join her on runs (though she won’t be running the race herself). “She’s my training partner,” Obiri says.

Thweatt is also Obiri’s first-ever female coach, and that’s not to be underestimated, either. “To have a female coach, you can't hide something from her,” Obiri says. “She already knows everything, what you're going through in your mind, in your body.”

Beyond running, Obiri does strength work three times per week, focusing on lower-body muscles like her calves and glutes, but surprisingly, she’s pretty focused on her arms, too. At her level, everything counts, including how strong your arms are when you’re swinging them during a race—an area that needs some improvement, she says.

She naps. Often. After her morning session, Obiri takes a snooze. Then, she heads to lunch. After lunch? She’s napping again. “I sleep a lot,” she says. Obiri estimates that she spends anywhere from five to six hours a day napping.

For Obiri, the basics—sleeping, eating, and hydrating—are the most important things for feeling her best. And when it comes to hydration, Obiri’s not getting caught up in the electrolyte craze or downing gallons of water. Instead, she relies on tea as her main source for fluids. She drinks all different kinds, but will make it in a big batch, complete with milk and three spoonfuls of sugar per cup.

“I’m addicted to tea with sugar,” she says. She has about seven cups per day, including before a run. It’s an easy way to get some extra carbs in, for sure. Along with her tea, before her 6:45 a.m. run, Obiri will have two slices of bread and a banana. “I can’t go on my runs with an empty stomach,” she says.

“The most important thing is to listen to your body,” she says. You might be feeling the excitement right off the bat or trying to keep up with the crowd, but remember to pay attention to how you feel and not go too hard too soon. “Don't go crazy because it's a marathon—it's a long journey—and needs patience,” she says. Make sure you’re keeping on top of fluids and fuel, too.

At this point, you may be deep into training and feeling drained—that’s completely normal, but does require a mindset shift. When Obiri is lacking motivation, she just tells herself she has to do it, or at least start it. “If I start, I will finish it,” she says. And, when a run gets hard? No matter how far she is from the end, she tells herself, “I’m almost there.”

It’s possible your For You Page (like mine) is filled with people freaking out about where they’re at in training—and it can be pretty easy to compare yourself to them. Maybe you have friends crushing long runs on Strava and are starting to wonder if it says anything about your progress.

Whatever it is, stay focused on your own program. “Everybody trains differently, so just know you have trained well and focus on your body, and trust me, you’ll be at the finish line and run well,” Obiri says.

Ultimately, your marathon is about you and what you did to get there. “Trust yourself, trust what you have been training for, and be ready to do what you have been training for six months or longer,” Obiri says.

Olivia Luppino is an associate editor at Women’s Health. She reports, writes, and edits content ranging from service stories to in-depth features and awards packages across all verticals, including health, fitness, sports, and beauty. While at WH, she’s traveled to Paris, France to watch Faith Kipyegon attempt a sub-4-minute mile and covered major races like Ultra Trail du Mont Blanc in Chamonix. Olivia is a RRCA-certified running coach who is especially passionate about helping people start their running journey and is training for her second marathon. #4976. Developing a Self-Talk Playbook

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

We talk to ourselves all day. This self-talk helps us to accomplish tasks, focus, and get motivated. Alternately, it can defeat us, sabotage us, and keep us from realizing our potential. What we say to ourselves is powerful and key to our ability to do just about everything.

Harnessing the power of our self-talk is a great performance optimization strategy to master. It improves both our physical and cognitive performance by building confidence, improving focus and concentration, increasing motivation, decreasing negative self-talk, and managing anxiety. Additionally, it can be deployed in the moment when we need to think quickly on our feet, pay close attention, or find that extra ounce of determination.

When we speak about performance improvement or enhancement, many people assume we are talking about athletes, pilots, and other elite performers. It’s true that elite performers are trained in the gambit of mental skills. However, these same psychological or mental skills are foundational for all of us. So—yes, self-talk can improve your professional tennis game, but it can also help to improve your attention, concentration, and emotional regulation; increase your motivation; and direct your energy toward essentially anything. So, whether you want to motivate yourself to do the dishes, get your application together for law school, improve your golf game, or ace flight training, self-talk is key.

Essentially, there are two kinds of self-talk linked to performance: instructional and motivational. They both serve to improve our performance, but in different ways. What follows is a basic guide to performance-enhancing self-talk and the information needed for you to develop your own self-talk playbook.

Instructional self-talk is what it sounds like. You walk yourself through a task or problem, often with the help of a memory aid such as a mantra or acronym, or provide yourself a simple reminder cue as to how to do something. These strategies allow you to focus on the current situation or task at hand, develop effective habits related to that specific task, and ensure that you follow correct procedures. Instructional self-talk is particularly powerful when learning a new skill, during an emergency, or when having to execute a complex task.

Most of us remember learning how to use a fire extinguisher through the use of the acronym PASS (Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep from side to side). Using the acronym more easily allows us to focus on the steps, execute the steps correctly, and gain self-control in an emergency situation. Likewise, if you’ve ever played sports, you’ve learned cues to remind you of the most effective ways to execute movements and plays.

Professions that involve high-risk and high-demand situations capitalize on instructional self-talk. Pilots and flight students, for example, know that during an emergency or task overload in the cockpit, to fall back on "Aviate, Navigate, Communicate" and then rely on the next checklist. Instructional self-talk improves cognitive and physical performance by providing direction, focusing attention, improving concentration, and helping to manage emotions.

Some simple rules of instructional self-talk include focusing on what to do, as opposed to what not to do, and keeping it relatively short and task-focused. During an emergency or if anxiety has crept in, taking one diaphragmatic breath can provide the pause you need to access your instructional self-talk and stay on track.

Motivational self-talk is also what it sounds like. You increase your focus, drive, and confidence in your own abilities to accomplish the task at hand, be that getting up off of the couch to go for a walk or instilling confidence in yourself during a high-stakes sporting event or training evolution. Motivational self-talk is best used in situations in which you need an extra dose of determination, or for an already mastered skill to enhance attentional control during execution of a task.

Studies have shown that for enhancing emotional regulation, third-person self-talk is more effective than speaking to yourself in the first person. Thus, “You got this!” may be a more effective example of motivational self-talk than “I got this!”

What motivational self-talk will work for you? Ask yourself, What would I say to a good friend who is in this same situation as I am? We tend to be kinder to our friends than to ourselves, and this allows us to better focus objectively on the task, making this an effective way to find exactly what you need. So: You can do this! Let's go! You have trained for this moment and are ready. Keep moving. (You get the idea.)

In conclusion, whether you need motivation to get started, the determination to keep going, or instructional cues to navigate a challenging task, self-talk is a powerful performance tool that is available anytime, anywhere. Like any mental skill, effective self-talk takes practice, but the payoff extends to virtually every aspect of your life. Start building your self-talk playbook by identifying a few simple instructional cues for important tasks and motivational phrases that work for you. Practice them, refine them, and put them to use. After all, if you're going to talk to yourself all day, you might as well make the conversation productive.

#4969. Chris Mottalini and His Son, Nino, Rediscover the Magic of Seeing the World Through a Child’s Eyes

Sal Charabi's temporary installation of lanterns in Giza

A lamp from his show Behind the Moon Mountain

Against the backdrop of Giza, architect/designer Salem Charabi just debuted fifteen lanterns in his first exhibition in Egypt—titled Behind the Moon Mountain and presented in the courtyard of his home/studio in the rural village of Al-Haraneya. Here, this past year, the Danish/Egyptian architect has made the Ramses Wissa Wassef Art Centre (founded in the early 1950s as a weaving school for children) a place of self-discovery. “The exhibition is the result of trying to uncover the landscapes that surround me,” says Charabi, who worked between Cairo and Copenhagen before moving to Egypt full-time in late 2025. “One of the luxuries of being from multiple places is the agility it gives you from a young age—the ability to rapidly adapt to your surroundings.” At the three-day installation, Charabi invited guests to observe the sun set and the lanterns come to life: The show’s title is inspired by the fable that the Nile springs from the Moon Mountains, an undefined range south of the country. Light in Egypt, he explains, is invoked continually as a blessing. When admiring something made by hand, one says, “May God illuminate your hands.” The 15 lanterns are made from hand-chiselled diorite from Aswan; palm reeds from date palms in Saqqara; and handmade paper made from the stems of banana palms in the Nile Delta. The lights also reference scenes of Cairo, a city of a million satellites, pigeon towers, and other improvised vertical structures. “I wanted to create an array of objects, derived from a type that changes and evolves with each iteration—illuminating the night, all exploring different proportions and scales. —Sam Cochran

Egypt's improvisational architecture inspired the lighting series.

Catalpa/Lightbulbs, a still life by AD contributing photographer Chris Mottalini and his son, Nino.

Pablo Picasso famously asserted, “It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.” The Spanish artist had lots to say about the struggle to recapture the magic and innocence of youth. Photographer Chris Mottalini, a frequent contributor to AD, found a shortcut in that journey, enlisting his son, Nino, as a collaborator on a project that has now spanned four years and two continents. “In 2022, when Nino was only five, I had the idea to task him with making sets out of paper, cardboard, and found objects for a new series of still-life images. I was just curious to see what he’d come up with,” Mottalini recalls. Nino accepted the challenge with gusto, unearthing oddities in the basement of the family’s home in the Hudson Valley, and foraging for foliage and flowers in the surrounding forest. The enterprise continued in Bangkok, the home of Nino’s maternal grandparents, where the budding artist discovered a wealth of antiques and toothsome Thai fruits. The results of their intriguing creative partnership are currently on view through November 15 at Available Items in Tivoli, New York, in an exhibition appropriately titled “Nino + Dad (Home Studies).” —Mayer Rus

A tablescape featuring Tabitha Simmons's new collection for Cabana

Fall is a time for leaf-peeping. The holidays are moments to raise a glass. Both traditions come to life in Tabitha Simmons’s new line of tableware for Cabana. Drawing upon classic English country house motifs, her own family memories, and the blazing colors of New England fall, the star designer has conjured a series of instant heirlooms. Oak leaves and acorns ring hand-painted plates. Embroidered placemats and napkins bear playful scalloped edges and foliate motifs. And a tablecloth reveals dense botanicals in a saturated hues of browns and crimson. You can all but smell the crisp autumn air. –Sam Cochran

#4966. In Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s North Carolina Home, Southern Hospitality Meets Modern Charm

The home was, decidedly, not love at first sight for Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick. “One of the rooms had caved in; there was water pouring in through the ceiling,” Decker says of the first time the couple saw the Charlotte, North Carolina, Georgian-style house.

But even in its dilapidated state, the 1960s-era home was still intriguing: It was located in the favored neighborhood for the young family, and its traditional, elegant proportions were still evident through its disrepair. At first it was Roddick, the former number-one men’s singles tennis player, who urged Decker to keep the house on their short list. Soon model and actor Decker, who grew up in nearby Matthews, warmed at the chance to rehabilitate a proper Carolina home with details like dental crown molding and classic brick. “We’d moved so many times [before this house],” she says. “And we were excited to try something new. For us, that meant a historic house with some old Southern bones.”

In the entry, Roddick is seated on a vintage sofa covered in a Zak and Fox fabric. Decker stands next to the walnut staircase built by Masterpiece Staircase and finished by Tony Montognese. The custom chandelier is by Kalin Asenov, the rug is vintage, and the artwork is by Kieran Brennan Hinton.

The family’s living room, clad in mahogany paneling, is Decker and Roddick’s favorite space in the whole home. The fireplace was designed by Decker, fabricated by Tyler Ernsberger, and stained by Tony Montognese, with animal carvings done by Stan Dunham. The 1930s coffee table is by Paul László, and the light fixture is a vintage Longobard for Poliarte. The chairs, clockwise from top right, are by BDDW, vintage Swedish sourced from PRB Collection, and a vintage Guglielmo Ulrich.

The home’s foyer received the biggest glow-up, with the staircase being entirely redesigned from a curving one. Chandelier and flush-mount light designed by Decker and Kalin Asenov, sideboard by BDDW, the mirror and sofa are vintage, millwork by Bill Truitt Woodworks (with finishes by Tony Montognese), and the walnut flooring is by Richard Marshall Fine Flooring.

Decker and Roddick were no strangers to home renovation, but as evidenced just from their first walkthrough, this latest undertaking would be on a scale they had not yet explored. The home had been little touched since its construction in 1964, and the couple would be only the second owners. Aside from obvious fixes like leaking ceilings and sagging floors, the layout, which was chopped up into a warren of tight quarters, needed a full gut to allow the space to breathe and gain more light. “We were parents of two young kids,” Decker says. “So the question was, How do we respect the grandeur of the house but also make it feel hospitable to a young family and one that can live up to the demands of everyday life?”

The dining room shows off many of the home’s thematic colors, including red, yellow, and green. Drapery fabric by Kravet, the pink chairs are vintage Kerstin Hörlin Holmquist, dining chairs by Studio Valle de Valle, antique farm table sourced from Obsolete, painting by Tyler Buck Guinn, and the pendants are by Of Enso, made with a vintage silk gingham from Decker’s personal collection.

The first-floor front room continues the nature theme thanks to its hand-painted custom mural. The sofa is a vintage Carl Malmsten upholstered in a Rose Uniacke fabric; the blue club chairs are vintage and sourced from Eneby Home; the leather chair is a vintage Hans Wegner; coffee table designed by Decker and fabricated by Dunham and Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry; and the armoire is a vintage walnut wet bar sourced from 1stDibs.

The kitchen hall’s allover paneling was fabricated by Bill Woodworks and installed by Blockhaus. Flush mounts by The Urban Electric Co.; the painting is a vintage William Skilling; sideboard by Bicyclette; and the rug is vintage found on Etsy.

The kitchen is painted in a muted shade of Decker’s favorite color: green. The double islands were designed by Decker and Dunham and fabricated by Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry; the pendants are by Roman and Williams Guild; the fittings by Waterworks; and the painting is an antique signed by Adelaide Briggs.

The breakfast nook brings the garden inside with its collection of plants and green accents. The table was custom-designed by Decker and Dunham and fabricated by Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry. The chairs are by Studio Ashby and upholstered with a Lee Jofa fabric, and the light fixture is a vintage Hans-Agne Jackobsson.

To help with the transformation, the couple engaged both Ruard Veltman Architecture for the architectural design and Stanwick Dunham for contracting. The group transformed the nearly 7,000-square-foot structure into a home that celebrates its lineage without being mired in the past. Nowhere is this effort more evident than in the gracious entryway, whose original carpeted staircase curved up from stark black and white tiles. And while that design wasn’t in poor taste, its severity read as both formal and cold. The solution was twofold: both to square-off the staircase and to clad the entire area in rich walnut paneling. The result not only allows sunlight to flow down from the second story, but showcases warm millwork. “We wanted it to look like it predated our arrival, and also be a bit more humble in its materials,” Decker says.

The primary bedroom’s wood floors and cream walls are softened up with the addition of a full wall of drapery, with fabric from William Morris. The chandelier is a vintage Carlo Scarpa sourced from 1stDibs, the bed from The Expert, linens from Nordic Knots, chair by Commune for George Smith, and the painting is by Alexandra Valenti.

Another view of the bedroom spotlights the family’s dog finding his light. Art by Tyler Hays Studio, nightstands by BDDW, vintage daybed from 1stDibs, and the vintage chair is sourced from Evan Reid.

The couple’s closet displays shoes almost in a museum-like setting, inside an antique French shoe cabinet sourced from 1stDibs. Ottoman from John Derian, the paint color is Farrow & Ball White Tie, and the chandelier is from RH.

The home’s primary bath was completely gut-renovated, but Decker wanted the design to appear original to the house. Tile from Waterworks, tub from Water Monopoly, side table by BDDW, painting by George Buckner of The Florida Highwaymen, and the pendant is an antique French copper lantern sourced from 1stDibs.

For the home’s interior design, Decker had no need of hiring a professional: She’s become a decorator herself. Over the last six or so years and mostly by word of mouth, the actor has spearheaded a variety of design projects (her latest, along with her design partners at By Idiots, being the interiors of Intown Golf Club’s new properties in Houston and Raleigh). For her family home, the brief was to keep the Georgian influence while updating the aesthetic. And it remains an evolving one: “Whenever I see that furniture dolly out, I know I’ll be involved at some point,” Roddick says.

Decker achieved the cozy yet elevated mix through color, using muted shades of green (her color), red, blue, and yellow; wallpaper with natural images like leaves or rivers; and plenty of vintage patterned rugs to soften up the wood floors. “It was originally old English meets early Georgian meets Shaker,” she says. “But when our kids became older, we really wanted to incorporate and take seriously what they wanted. Because, how cool to be eight and actually have some say in the space around you? So now the house is a hodgepodge of explosive color, a lot of which is totally inspired and dictated by them.”

The children’s playroom has a vintage feel while still being cozy. Sofa by RH, mohair chair and ottoman by Sam Klemick, wallpaper by Charles Voysey, and the shades are Fabricut fabric.

The couple’s daughter wanted her new room to match her softball team’s colors of red, white, and blue. Bed designed by Decker and fabricated by Liven UP, vintage chandelier sourced from PRB Collection, drapes from Anthropologie, and the rug is sourced from Hall Pass Vintage.

Decker’s office adds a bit of whimsy with a ceiling papered in a Pierre Frey design. Rug by Studio MRS for Nordic Knots, sofa by Coley Home, the desk is vintage, and the chandelier is by Apparatus.

An upstairs landing is one of Decker’s favorite places to snuggle with the family pets. Pendant by Roman and Williams Guild, dresser by Orior, the chairs are vintage Paolo Buffa upholstered in a Rose Uniacke fabric, table is vintage sourced from PRB Collection, and the pillows were made by Chancery Custom with vintage tapestry fabric sourced by Decker.

#4965. Finding Your Way: Signage Still Matters

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Two recent encounters with wayfinding problems reinforce my belief that good (that is, effective) signage still matters. With the advent and dominance of GPS systems and mobile apps, some people think that being able to find your way is a snap. It isn’t, especially when you are on foot.

Consider this outdoor example from my hometown. I was in my bank parking lot, which borders a busy street, and a woman across the parking lot called out, “Excuse me, can you tell me where the restrooms are?” At first I couldn’t imagine what she meant, but then she continued. “They told me the restrooms are next to the parking lot,” and then she pointed away from where we were standing and down the street. I surmised that she had asked someone waiting in a long line to get into a popular local bakery and was directed to the public restrooms, which do in fact exist and are adjacent to one of two parking lots nearby. There was a restroom sign posted on the street, but it was difficult to see amidst what I will call “signage clutter,” and the arrow on the sign wasn’t easy to make out. I walked over to her and pointed down the street, to the brick restrooms adjacent to the entry to a museum parking lot (see photo).

In this case, her wayfinding problem was solved by assistance from a human being (me) with knowledge of the area. As we all know, human beings with wayfinding knowledge are not always available.

Let’s take an indoor case. Many wayfinding problems occur in healthcare facilities (and a lot of other places, such as office buildings). A major reason for such problems is that the rabbit warren of corridors in those buildings and the complexity of the structure make providing adequate signage for all possible destinations a real challenge. Doing so can result in information overload (i.e., too much information to process). Typically, hospitals have a repetition of elements (e.g., corridors) that look the same, and the building sections have grown incrementally, often into a shape that would not have been recommended for ease of navigation. Thus, while general hospitals may have been planned to create legible (i.e., understandable) spaces, their pattern of growth often creates spatial configurations that are hard to support with signage.

In the current example, I was visiting a relative who had undergone a knee replacement, and when I entered the lobby, the receptionist handed me a piece of paper that said:

As an environmental psychologist and someone who focused on wayfinding earlier in my career, I had to shake my head when handed this piece of paper. If the signage in healthcare facilities were really good, would we need these paper aids? Yet, in all fairness to the facilities, there are many people who need such assistance (e.g., people with memory problems). It is also the case that people visiting healthcare facilities are generally anxious, even if just visiting, which decreases memory function.

You may be thinking, "What's the big deal? It's just a minor inconvenience to have to ask for directions to a restroom or in a hospital or to avoid being late for an appointment." But the consequences of effective signage can be far more important.

In 2016, a woman named Laura Levis having an asthma attack died outside a hospital emergency room in Massachusetts when she could not find an open entrance. As a result of this tragedy, what is known as Laura’s Law became signed legislation in 2021. Its goal is to address the need for effective signage in hospitals, and the Department of Public Health in Massachusetts is charged with implementing statewide standards for improving lighting, signage, wayfinding, and other elements connected to patient access to emergency rooms in Massachusetts. As soon as an individual is on the hospital campus, directional signs to the ER must be available (Dwyer, 2023).

Wayfinding systems often have been viewed as an after-the-fact application—in other words, something that is overlaid on the environment after the structure is complete (Devlin, 2014). And while we may eventually have mobile applications widely available in indoor environments for wayfinding use in hospitals, that is not currently the case (Morag & Pintelon, 2021), although a number of hospitals, including Johns Hopkins and Boston Children’s Hospital, use digital wayfinding. Such mobile applications for wayfinding are more common in commercial environments. Johns Hopkins notwithstanding, you are more likely to currently find wayfinding support such as electronic directories and interactive kiosks in healthcare environments.

And if you need convincing that signage is an afterthought, consider this example from NYC (see photo, left).

It is clear we are headed in the direction of increasing reliance on technology to help us find our way. But is there a cost in terms of our cognitive function? For example, is there a negative impact of GPS on spatial cognition? Some cross-sectional research by Dahmani and Bohbot (2020) suggests that people who have a greater lifetime experience using GPS perform more poorly when asked to do a wayfinding task without the use of GPS. Moreover, in a small follow-up (i.e., longitudinal) study, those who had greater reliance on GPS since the first data collection showed a greater drop-off in spatial memory that depends on the hippocampus. Yet we shouldn’t jump to the conclusion that GPS use has a necessary negative impact on actual wayfinding skill. While a 2024 meta-analysis of 23 studies (Miola et al., 2024) showed a negative association of environmental knowledge with GPS use and also a negative association with self-reported sense of direction, there was no statistically significant association with wayfinding performance.

As we become more and more absorbed by our technological devices for wayfinding such as smartphones and their mobile apps, we should not forget the value of simply looking around our environment. Yes, designers need to devote more time and energy to creating effective wayfinding systems, but there is great value in visually engaging with our surroundings. Not only will this likely result in better wayfinding experiences, but it will also remind us that our surroundings have the capacity to surprise and fascinate us. We have to look around to know that.

#4960. 14 Best Airbnbs in the South of France for Bucolic Romance (2026)

The South of France has long been shorthand for bucolic romance. The region has drawn painters, film stars, and sun-starved travelers for generations, seducing them with endless vineyards and lavender fields, sleepy medieval villages, and its glittering Riviera. From Provence to the Côte d’Azur, the south of France offers a storybook mélange of rustic farmhouses, centuries-old castles and estates, along with honey-hued stone houses tucked into timeless hilltop towns.

Whether you fancy swimming in a pool besides your own château, late evening pétanque games at a centuries-old castle, gathering a group of friends at a hillside estate, or cozying up in a rustically romantic village apartment, Airbnb has options for turning every south of France fantasy into a reality. Here are some of the most extraordinary homes for rent in the region—spots so tempting, you might just want to cancel your return ticket and settle in for a year in Provence.

Perks: Mountain views, lake access, sauna, balcony, hot tub, indoor and outdoor fireplaces, pool table

While the South of France may be synonymous with summer, this contemporary chalet makes a compelling case for a winter escape with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame Sancy Valley’s mountain views. There’s plenty of room for up to 10 guests to spread out in this five bedroom home with a generous living space that includes three bathrooms and a pool table. Tucked in the hilly countryside, proximity to both Alpine and Nordic skiing is the property’s main draw for those looking to hit the slopes. After a day spent outside, both the indoor fireplace or sauna provide a perfect spot to warm up, though you could also enjoy the fresh air on the expansive balcony while keeping toasty by the outdoor fireplace or hot tub. From $1,048 per night.

Perks: Private backyard, fireplace, sound system, fully-equipped kitchen, security system, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

Located at the foot of Signal du Mailhebiau in the Aubrac region, this two-bedroom getaway is immersed in its rural landscape, surrounded by rolling fields, grazing cattle, and the French Countryside’s natural beauty. Originally built as a buron, or shepherd’s hut, the home has been thoughtfully transformed into a modern retreat that celebrates its architectural history. Hand-laid stone walls, vaulted ceilings, and a loft preserve the structure’s rustic character, while a dramatic wall of windows introduces a contemporary counterpoint, framing picturesque views of the expansive countryside. From $484 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, outdoor dining area, free parking, breakfast baskets delivered by request

Once the orangery of a stately chateau, this converted studio apartment retains its romantic design with soaring ceilings, a wall of French doors, and cheerful green-and-white checkerboard floor. Today, the space is an elegant retreat for two (or a couple with a baby thanks to the available crib), whether you’re spending leisurely afternoons indoors, sipping wine on the terrace, or exploring the surrounding vineyards and forests. For those looking to wander or partake in the region’s rich wine history, you’re about a 30-minute drive to the center of Bordeaux. From $165 per night.

Perks: Vineyard views, pool, outdoor shower, private backyard, fully-equipped kitchen, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

This isn’t so much a home to stay in as a castle to occupy. Situated on nearly ten acres of private parkland, this spacious 16th century château sleeps eight, while an additional two cottages can accommodate another eight guests. A large swimming pool, sun-drenched terrace, and lawn dotted with cypress trees practically beg you to throw a summer soirée. Inside, Château du Hameau’s historic bones remain prominent with original stone flooring, sweeping stairway, and ornate coiffured ceilings. With multiple fireplaces, soaking tubs, and seemingly endless views of fields and vineyards, this is a place to dream about long after you leave. From $1,825 per night.

Perks: Private tennis court, private pool, concierge service

Rustic architecture meets contemporary comfort at the sprawling Mas de l’Aiguebrun Estate, a super-sized stay with enough space to house up to 15 lucky guests. Old world design features like exposed brick and wood beam ceilings that date back to the 11th century contrast modern amenities like a La Cornue oven, waterfall showers, and even a mini rock climbing wall to entertain younger guests. The property has a prime location in Bonnieux, a village with an abundance of restaurants and cafes, as well as a Friday morning market that visitors swear by for local produce and baked goods. Back at the Airbnb, you’re encouraged to spend sunny days en plein air taking advantage of the picturesque outdoor amenities, which include an impressive stone-carved outdoor dining setup, 20-meter swimming pool, and a red clay tennis court to channel your inner Nadal. From $2,150 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, updated air conditioning, complimentary tea and coffee

Natural light floods this 16th century townhouse located in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, a village whose most famous residents include the likes of Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse. Beautiful interiors are expected when your host is an interior designer, and this property delivers spatial excellence with considered details like a restrained color palette, layered textures, and contemporary furnishings. The combined kitchen and dining area is a perfect place to enjoy slow mornings (in fact, we think the envy-inducing pottery shelf is an idea you’ll want to recreate in your own space). A copper bath tub faces a king-sized bed in one of the main bedrooms, complete with a window view overlooking the surrounding foliage. For more private guests, the property also has three en suite bathrooms in a glassy green color palette, each housing their own tubs and showers. If you’re hoping to explore your charming provincial surroundings, lots of art and shopping attractions await; plus, the 40-minute drive to Nice makes it convenient to plan a day trip or two. From $649 per night.

Gilded light fixtures, muted textiles, and farmhouse furniture all distinguish this abundantly pastoral stay on the French Riviera. While there’s plenty of classic provincial charm to immerse yourself in—exposed wood beams, stone flooring, and two fireplaces—the design also ties in moments of splashy Mediterranean character with coastal furnishings and colorful tilework. It’s worth stopping by the local markets to gather ingredients for a meal or two in the fully-equipped kitchen, with its pine green cabinetry, Smeg stove and matching dishwasher, as well as a dishware collection rounded out by plenty of Serax ceramics for a festive dinner party. When you are looking to venture out, the surrounding Roquefort les Pins offers a small community of indie stores run by locals, and eateries, while more lively attractions in Nice, Antibes, and Cannes are just a 30 minute drive away. From $693 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, pétanque court, chef, cleaners, and airport transfer available upon request, close to wineries and a golf course

This nine-bedroom complex sleeps a crowd, but no matter how many people you arrive with, you’re bound to be struck by the ultra-private feeling of the estate. The centuries-old stone buildings surrounded by cypress trees originally comprised a farm, but today have been converted into three buildings fit for at least 16 guests. Inside, the oversized rooms are filled with cushy leather couches, bentwood chairs, and cozy beds. Outdoors, the scenic grounds are just right for a heated game of pétanque or a dip in the heated pool. From $2,894 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, air conditioning, indoor fireplace, crib, cleaning available during your stay, pizza oven

If you’ve been daydreaming of your very own French estate, it’s entirely possible you’ve manifested this Airbnb into being. Nestled in the Provençal countryside near the village of Gordes, the 12-bedroom home offers striking mountain views alongside a range of picturesque outdoor perks that include a heated pool, pétanque court, and an elegant garden. The home’s original features have been thoughtfully maintained, from the exposed stone walls to the vaulted ceilings, while the interiors lean into pastoral elegance with farmhouse furnishings and creamy linens. Not too far from the villa, you can traipse through the infamous lavender fields and vineyards that have become synonymous with the region. From $959 per night.

Perks: Ocean-front views, central AC, swimming pool, security system

This palatial estate on the French Riviera might be large enough for a royal wedding, but that doesn’t mean you can’t book the six-bedroom home all for yourself. Everything about this rental is over-the-top, from the palm trees that flank the front door to the grand entry hall complete with marble columns, a sweeping staircase, and ceiling frescos. Staying here feels a bit like having a castle all to yourself, one where you can while away the days outside in the gardens, by the pool, or along the nearby shores. The grand, high-ceilinged spaces interiors are outfitted with antique furnishings and chandeliers, along with an elective blend of mid-century pieces and lots of artwork. Should the mood strike for a soirée fit for a king, the home’s living room and conservatory can easily accommodate 200 for a cocktail party. From $10,350 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, extensive grounds, heated pool, cleaning available during your stay

For those “go big or go home” vacations, go ahead and book a grand castle. This one is from the 17th century and encompasses over 300 acres of forest, farmland, and vineyards. The property itself features nine bedrooms, most which have ensuite bathrooms with soaking tubs, terracotta and stone floors, exposed stone walls, and bright and airy rooms doused in bright colors like marigold to cerulean. Inside and out, there are multiple seating areas, including a music room and dedicated office, to gather with guests (accommodating over a dozen people at any given time). From $2,458 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, piano, washer and dryer, pool, EV charger, exercise equipment, pool and pink pong tables, outdoor dining area

This sprawling farmhouse just outside the village of Mouriès sleeps at least 16 people and has plenty of room, both inside and out, for everyone to sprawl out. #4957. Influencers Are Doing ‘Olive Oil Shots.’ We Asked 4 Experts If That’s a Good Idea—and They All Basically Said the Same Thing.

The truth about the supposed health practice—revealed.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

SO OLIVE OIL shots are a thing again. Remember in the mid- to late-2010s, when people were knocking back all manner of liquids, including apple cider vinegar, juiced ginger, pulverized turmeric, and extra virgin olive oil? Well, social media influencers have brought back at least the last one, with Bryan Johnson doing “evo” shots and Steven Gundry, MD, recommending a daily dose of the stuff. (Also, both those guys sell their own olive oil. Just saying.)

The supposed benefits of shooting olive range from the more generalized “more energy” to more specific ones, like protecting your cardiovascular system from disease.

Influencers usually back up these claims by citing scientific research on the benefits of adding olive oil to your daily diet. But do the benefits extend to doing shots of olive oil?

“Olive oil is great for heart health and contains beneficial polyphenols, but you don't need to take it as a shot. You get the same benefits by just including it in your meals, and it's generally much more enjoyable that way. But if you want to take it as a shot, there's no harm in that. It's just not superior to including olive oil in your diet in regular ways. You know, with food.”

“I'm a fan of California Olive Ranch 100% California Extra Virgin Olive Oil For Everyday. It's high quality, reasonably affordable (for evoo), and widely available. I use it to saute veggies, roast tubers and veggies, and drizzle on various things.”

“I'm a bigger fan of eating a few shots of olive oil with sauteed veggies or I pour it on my food. But a shot is fine I guess. People like to do it in the longevity scene to invoke ancient Greeks doing shots of ‘liquid gold.’”

“I am an affiliate of the Fresh Pressed Olive Oil Club, which I reallly love. I've not had lots of fancy, fresh olive oils from around the world before and now I have. I like seeing and tasting the diversity. I use a 1-liter glass bottle of EVOO, usually Braggs or Whole Food Organic. I try to go through two to three of these a month for our house of four.”

“I wouldn’t suggest shots of olive oil for any reason. All that’s happening here is that you’re adding a concentrated source of calories and fat to your diet. There are no documented benefits of doing this for the average person, and it can cause weight gain if the oil shots are taken in addition to someone’s current diet. This can ultimately cause health problems.”

“I don’t really have a fave oil. I use brands that have a seal of origin in them to ensure their purity.”

“While olive oil is full of beneficial compounds that may support heart health and longevity, shooting it isn't necessary. Heating olive oil may degrade some beneficial polyphenols, but using it as a salad dressing, sauce, or finishing oil for roasted veggies provides the same benefits, plus enhanced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids.”

“Extra-virgin olive oil can have such a range of flavors. I love San Giuliano Coastal Harvest Olive Oil. It's cold-pressed, which helps preserve more nutrients and polyphenols, and has a really nice, peppery flavor. While I don't take shots of it, I regularly use it in dressings and over veggies.”

Paul Kita is a Deputy Editor at Men's Health, where he has covered food, cooking, nutrition, supplements, grooming, tech, travel, and fatherhood at the brand for more than 15 years. He is also the author of two Men's Health cookbooks, Guy Gourmet and A Man, A Pan, A Plan, and the winner of a James Beard Award.

#4955. The Best Dining Room Lighting Ideas to Set Your Space Aglow

As romantic as candlelight dining sounds, it’s simply not practical (way too much wax!). The best dining room lighting ideas are thoughtfully planned: They take your actual eating habits, furniture proportions, room structure, and budget into consideration. They weigh the benefits of pendant lights vs. chandeliers vs. flush mounts and wall sconces, not to mention bulb type.

Lighting, it turns out, gets pretty involved—which is why we’ve tapped interior designers from around the country for their brightest ideas. And though the considerations are complex, modern lighting can be just as romantic as the candlelight option. “The evolving landscape is opening the door to more thoughtful layers and innovative ideas for how lighting can shape a space,” says Mike Shively of Chicago-based AD PRO firm En Masse Architecture and Design. “Lighting and coziness are both things we associate with luxury today, and neither necessarily comes down to price.”

In fashion designer Marysia Reeves’s Venice Beach home, a breezy, lantern-like fixture hovers above the wood dining table.

Pendant lighting gets more playful when each piece hangs at a different height. The look works especially well with a vaulted ceiling, as evidenced by this dining room set in a pavilion at the back of the house. “A cluster of glass pendants hung at staggered heights works alongside a pair of table lamps on the sideboard to create warm, layered light,” says Lucas Goldbach of En Masse Architecture and Design, who worked on the project.

The varying heights of the pendants gives this light fixture some dimension.

In this stunner of an LA home by design collective the Archers, a Le Corbusier–inspired table is lit with simple can overhead lights (definitely dimmable versions).

Lighting options are about more than just form. A more traditional shape can look entirely new when cast in a surprising material. “Our recommendation is to rethink conventional finishes and materials wherever possible,” says Sarah Goesling of Goesling Group, an AD PRO Directory firm based in Chicago. “For a chain-mail fixture, look beyond stainless steel to a striking yellow gold. For braided metal hardware, trade the ruggedness of wrought iron for the refined sheen of polished gunmetal.”

For a dining room in a midcentury-modern home, Goesling Group chose an appropriately retro 1950s-inspired Nabila chandelier by Tooy. And to add a modernized touch through the materials, they went with smoked glass around the bulbs.

A Sputnik-style fixture draws the eye up in this dining room by Goesling Group.

If you find an antique fixture you love, it might be worth rewiring the piece. Source on sites like eBay, Etsy, and 1stdibs, or take a lap around your local flea market. Alternatively, scour relatives’ attics and basements for a fixture with some family history. In the dining room below, designed by En Masse Architecture and Design, the light fixture was originally bought by the homeowner’s parents and was refurbished by Archistoric. “It became the inspiration for many of the metal finishes used throughout the new design,” says Goldbach.

This En Masse Architecture and Design dining space is crowned by an heirloom chandelier, refurbished by Archistoric.

Sconces, floor lamps, even table lamps can do the job of overhead pendant and flush-mount fixtures—so don’t force one if you’re not sure you like the look at all (proof, via Amélie Colombet’s apartment).

Fixtures made from natural alabaster stone are popular because of the warm, glare-free glow they emit. And because the translucent material has natural veining, no two pieces are alike. You can find alabaster in a variety of shapes—including linear forms, mini pendants, and semi-flush-mount ceiling lights—and while it’s generally pretty pricey (ranging anywhere from $300 for a single alabaster pendant lamp to $3,000 for a row of pendants), it’s also a durable material that lasts.

In the dining nook below, designed by Goesling Group, the minimal fixture makes a major impression. “It’s a solid alabaster stone piece lit all the way around the rim that looks like the moon when it glows,” says Goesling.

The pendant sets a striking tone in this cozy dining nook by Goesling Group.

If you have no interest in hardwiring a thing . . .Get an arc floor lampYou can have proper overhead lighting for your dining area without hardwiring a thing overhead. All you need is an arc floor lamp; they plug right into a wall outlet but stand tall, with a long, curved neck that will position the bulb and shade directly over your table. (How’s that for simplified?) The Arco floor lamp by Flos is a classic, but more budget-conscious shoppers can spring for similar styles from retailers like Wayfair (or even Amazon!).

If you’re trying to decide between options . . .Take the shape and style of your table into considerationThe overhead fixture you choose and the table itself “don’t have to [have] a direct geometrical correlation, but there should be some proportional consideration,” says Russell Groves of New York City–based Groves & Co. A long or unusually large chandelier would obviously overpower a short table, and vice versa: A teeny-tiny bulb might look silly above a big table. Same goes for the look: A lovely old farmhouse table would do well with a lovely farmhouse fixture or something super-modern for contrast—but either way, they should be considered together.

If you’d like to jazz up a fixture you already own . . .Customize the lampshadeA reflective material inside the shade will help cast light back down toward the table, Groves points out, while perforated shades will turn any bulb into a twinkly light (if that’s your prerogative). “Textured fabrics like raw silk will add a beautiful warmth and shadow to a room,” he says, but should you require a more directional cast, “an opaque shade wouldn’t give you a lot of glow in the room but would put more on the table.” Just because a fixture has shades you’re not into doesn’t mean it’s the end of the line. Swap them out!

If you’re sick of the typical dining room look . . .Consider less-traditional fixtures“Unreal times call for surreal styles, and lighting is emerging as a particularly compelling canvas for experimentation,” says Goesling. “From blown-glass designs with off-kilter stripes, to chain-mail, tapestry, and wrought iron reimagined through unexpected finishes and geometric patterns, these materials and techniques are taking on a new life. We anticipate seeing this influence extend across lighting, from woven metal sheaths and illustrative shades to sculptural, cast forms.”

A unique accent light sometimes even doubles as art. Such is the case in a Chicago penthouse designed by Kuchar, which features a dining room fixture with a strikingly sinuous form. “Going for the cool, funky light fixture has become the new normal among our residential clients,” says Sarah Kuchar-Parkinson, owner and creative director of the Chicago-based studio. “Not only does it bring brightness and light, but it adds architectural interest and an element of quirk.”

A statement-making light fixture hovers above the dining room table of this Kuchar-designed Chicago penthouse.

When hanging a pendant or a chandelier . . .Take care to hang it at the correct heightToo high and a pendant lamp might look stuck to the ceiling, constricted; too low and you won’t be able to see your guests around it. Somewhere in between is just right, so step back and consider it at various lengths before settling on one. “When you’re seated, you don’t want [the fixture] to be in your face—the same way everyone gets annoyed when flowers are in the way,” Groves says.

If you’re into geometric lines . . .Get creative with the cordWhen hanging a pendant lamp with a very simple silhouette, feel free to get creative with the cord: Zigzag it from wall to wall around a corner, tack it in swags along the ceiling, or loop it over a hook on the wall.

To soften overly bright overheads . . .Add a dimmerDesigner Sam Allen of Sam Allen Interiors, based in Weston, Connecticut, feels strongly about the worth of a dimmer switch: “If your dining room chandelier is not hooked up to a dimmer, call an electrician right now. I mean it. Don’t even finish reading this—call your electrician first.” With the simple pressing of a lever or turning of a knob, dimmable lighting allows you to control the brightness of the bulbs, which is particularly important if you’re dealing with often-harsh overhead lighting. “To me, chandeliers should mimic candlelight,” says Groves—and that warm, dim glow is possible if you just install dimmers. Plus, they’re available in both modern and traditional silhouettes that will add considerably more charm to the walls than those plastic switch plates you hate anyway.

To make the room multifunctional . . .Supplement the lighting solution you chooseIf you end up setting your table with some nice, warm candlelight, you might need to add sconces or downlights to supplement that glow when the room is used for anything other than an intimate dinner. (Dining room tables are very good for DIY projects, we’d like to note.) And to up a room’s cozy factor, lean into lamps. “The more lamps the better,” says Goldbach. “We like using smaller-scale lamps and vintage pieces in unexpected ways to create a warm, layered atmosphere. Multiple light sources can make the space feel cozier and more inviting, especially as the days get shorter.”

If you’re a fanatic about light quality . . .Be selective with the bulbsWarm white light, cool light, bright light—you can get exactly the brightness level you desire with the right bulb. For lots of ambience, try vintage-inspired filament bulbs. If it’s more of a particular shape and style you’re after for an exposed-bulb fixture, try decorative bulbs. And for the ultimate in energy efficiency, invest in LED bulbs, which are up to 90 percent more efficient than traditional light bulbs.

#4953. How to Set Boundaries Without the "Who Started It" Fight

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Often, when a client sits down on the couch and wants to tell a recent story about a relationship, they go back. Sometimes way back, even decades. The current event is just another brick in a wall that the client seems to carry on their back wherever they go.

In a way, it makes sense. If you want to solve a problem, it is only reasonable to track it to its beginning, take care of the roots, and let the rest follow. But the reality of relationships is often much more complicated than that. Our memories differ, and each person in the relationship often holds a different story close to their heart and can swear it is the only real truth. At times, these stories are only somewhat different, and at other times they are completely contradictory.

In research about interpersonal conflict, Baumeister and his colleagues explained that "Autobiographical narratives… can be considered as the product of negotiation between actual events and desired self-concepts." That is, regardless of whether we perceive ourselves as the victim or the perpetrator in a given situation or relationship, "people can be induced to act in ways that at least mildly contradict their preferred beliefs about themselves. Rather than regarding these incidents as proof that they are immoral, weak, gullible, or otherwise lacking in virtue, people may rationalize the events by constructing stories that are more compatible with their preferred views of themselves."

This rationalization might help us build a story about ourselves, the relationship, and life that we can live with, but it won't necessarily help us thrive. While we might feel that we have a good understanding of the story, how it started and who did what to whom, the other side of the relationship might hold an entirely different one.

In Baumeister's research, participants were asked to write about a time when they made someone angry and about a time when someone made them angry. When people wrote from the victim's perspective, they described the other person's behavior as arbitrary and hard to understand, and they added the event to a longer chain in the history of the relationship. When people wrote as the perpetrator, they described their own behavior as reasonable and framed the event as single and closed. The researchers suggest that conflicts often arise when one side holds in their anger and accumulates frustration over time until they eventually react, while the other person only experiences the explosion and sees it as an out-of-proportion reaction.

Often, we are waiting for permission, from ourselves or from the people around us, to set a boundary that will protect us. We hold on to our story, telling and retelling it, because we think this is what will allow us to draw the line, to step back, to stop negotiating.

But we don't have to. We can set our boundaries without waiting for an external, objective verdict that will never come and use our internal strength and judgment to decide what we are willing to accept from other people and how to protect ourselves when the line is crossed. It doesn't have to depend on the past.

Instead of asking "Who started this?" you can ask "What do I need right now to feel safe in this relationship?" or "What am I no longer willing to do?" These questions don't require the other side to approve your version of the story or to allow you to act as you think is appropriate.

That being said, this doesn't mean that the past has no meaning, or that the history of the relationship isn't affecting what it is now. You can take history into account, remember things, and still act in the present without full resolution.

Sometimes, it might be helpful to let go of the origin story and stay in the present. You don't have to ask for permission or prove you were a victim. You are allowed to set your boundaries.

Baumeister, R. F., Stillwell, A., & Wotman, S. R. (1990). Victim and perpetrator accounts of interpersonal conflict: Autobiographical narratives about anger. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(5), 994. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.59.5.994

Share this post Facebook Bluesky Linkedin Email

Yael Hallak is a NY Licensed Mental Health Counselor, researcher at The New School’s Gender & Health Lab, and journalist at Haaretz writing about women, health, and the psychology of self-control.
