#4866. 11 Best Love Seats for Small Spaces That Are Stylish (2026)

The most inviting living spaces have comfortable, functional seating options—but you don’t need a room big enough for a sprawling sectional to establish that welcoming vibe. Instead, turn to a small-space–friendly love seat, a compact sofa designed for two people, hence the name.

Even if you don’t live in a tiny apartment, a small sofa can add a romantic je ne sais quoi to a room, making a space feel more intimate, especially if you select a style with a curvy backrest that envelops guests like a hug. If you do have the space, pairing your love seat with a chaise or accent chairs can extend the footprint and add even more seating options while providing more opportunity to elevate the room’s design. One look at the vintage love seat that lives in Usher’s Atlanta home will make you a believer.

Here, find 11 designs, all between 55 and 70 inches wide, to accommodate all tastes, including the iconic mod Knoll womb settee and the more traditional leather love seat from Crate & Barrel.

Why settle for a traditional silhouette when you can have a bit of fun with your love seat? The West Elm Bogart style caught contributor Lori Keong’s eye because of its elegant bolstered back with rounded arms and a sculptural cutout base that conceals the legs. “No blocky, chubby legs or ugly hairpin appendages to stare at while I vacuum….what a concept!” she says in her review. Initially, she had some reservations about it being too stiff, classifying it as feeling similar to a medium-firm mattress. “It’s definitely firm and supportive but also not rock-hard, with just enough give—and no sag—to sleep or sit on comfortably.” Keong chose the alabaster basketweave, but if that color-upholstery combination doesn’t fit your space or style, now you can choose from 79 other options.

Serena & Lily wears the crown for coastal decor, but its offerings extend far beyond predictable patterns of sky pinstripes and gingham. With more than 125 upholstery options available—including linen, basketweave, cotton, denim, and more—in solid colors and patterns, the Spruce allows you to dress up the classic silhouette to fit a home of any style. If the slipcover is not your thing, the alternative is introducing exposed wood legs in four colorways. Regardless of your decor, the solid wood frame of this compact love seat is built to last.

For its boucle love seat, Quince uses performance fabric that is Oeko-Tex–certified, a designation that the textile in question is free of dangerous levels of harmful substances. Beneath the cozy, nubby fabric, foam cushions are supported by a hardwood frame, which is FSC-certified—a credential from the Forest Stewardship Council that specifies responsible wood sourcing. The combination of curvy, clean lines, and ivory color gives this two-seater an elevated elegance without a hefty price tag.

The Crate & Barrel Axis love seat comes in an astounding 45 leather options, including more traditional hues like caramel and bold burgundy and statement-making onyx. Silicone-based vegan materials are also available. The look, anchored by track arms and an angled back, is classic and can work just as well in an entryway as it would in a den.

The Pottery Barn Cameron power-reclining sofa may make you forget that you opted for a love seat at all. Once you hit the power button to recline and stretch out, you’ll forget all about this modular sofa’s compact stature. If your space can accommodate a few extra inches, consider adding a storage compartment between the seats for a spot to stash a mid-movie snack. Plus, the modular nature of this couch’s design means it can shift and grow with you, should you decide to place it elsewhere in your home or move to a new space altogether.

The Sabai Essential love seat looks like a hug. The low-profile seat with bench seating and plush back cushions practically begs for late-night reading sessions. Lounging is also sweeter when you know that the recycled polyester velvet is Oeko-Tex–certified as well as Global Recycled Standard 4.0-verified, a certification that affirms the content of recycled materials. And if you end up loving the seat too much, you can make use of the brand’s Repair Don’t Replace program that allows you to revive various components, like a single cushion or a scuffed sofa leg. Alternatively, if you prefer to refresh the upholstery du jour, simply swap it for a new slipcover at a fraction of the cost of a new love seat.

Joybird is the place to find a modern love seat, especially one that will go with your colorful wallpaper. The Amelia style is curvy with a twist: Its 1970s-inspired frame has a suave shape, but the cushions retain the expected rectangular configuration. Available in an eye-popping 91 colors, you should do yourself a favor and order the swatch sample box to help you choose. At 56.5 inches wide, it’s one of the smaller love seats on this list, making it ideal for teeny-tiny alcoves and nooks.

The AllModern Rae love seat comes in velvet and linen textures, giving you flexibility on whether you prefer a dressier or more casual style. Regardless of the upholstery choice, the channel stitching detail on the arms gives this compact love seat a contemporary look. The fabric is stain- and spill-resistant, but it is spot-clean–only. However, its reversible cushions let you hide a one-off oops. Also nice is that at just under 100 pounds, it’s a relatively easy sofa to move around by yourself. Toss in a few throw pillows, and you’ve got a whole new look.

Just looking at the CB2 Deseo makes us want to flop down and relax atop the two giant, pillow-like cushions filled with feathers and down. With a whopping 82 options for upholstery type and color, you can customize the love seat to fit into any room: Go for an opulent look with a rich merlot color, or tropical with the lsla Royal banana leaf linen-cotton for your sunroom.

Knoll earmarked a spot in the history of design with the Womb settee by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen, who said in 1948, “Today, more than ever, we need to relax.” Nearly 80 years later, the statement still rings true. It took Saarinen two years to make this chair, but from there, production didn't stop. Adding this piece to your furniture collection basically makes it an heirloom.

Take a page out of Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s Charlotte, North Carolina, entryway that features a small sofa with a back made of unexpected arches. The Lulu and Georgia Aimee Song Neve sofa surprises with its artfully sculpted seats that—at a medium on the firmness scale—are all about comfort. Among many upholstery and color options, it’s available in chunky boucle and garnet-and-blue stripe—a color combo that’s designer-approved.

#4865. Segway launches the $1,999 Xyber Air, bringing its futuristic moped-style e-bike to the masses

When Segway launched the original Xyber last year, it was one of those e-bikes that immediately turned heads. With its futuristic styling, oversized frame, and high-performance off-road ambitions, it looked more like a concept vehicle than something you could actually buy.

Now the company is hoping to capture a much wider audience with the new Segway Xyber Air, a lighter, street-legal version that keeps much of the original’s aggressive styling while fitting neatly into the familiar Class 1, 2, and 3 e-bike categories.

At first glance, you’d be forgiven for mistaking the Xyber Air for its larger sibling. It retains the angular frame design and moto-inspired proportions that made the original stand out, complete with Segway’s signature X-shaped front and rear lighting.

But beneath the familiar styling is a much more approachable machine.

Power comes from a 750W nominal rear hub motor producing 80 Nm of torque, with peak output reaching 1,600W.

Riders can choose between Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 operation depending on local regulations, with speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in Class 1 and 2 modes or 28 mph (45 km/h) in Class 3.

Segway has even included a Hybrid Mode that allows throttle operation up to 20 mph while pedal assist continues to 28 mph without requiring riders to switch between ride modes.

That’s still kosher in many states, but some are starting to require true Class 3 e-bikes to have no throttle operation at all, so check your local regulations to make sure you’re compliant.

The bike is powered by a 717 Wh battery that Segway claims can deliver up to 58 miles (93 km) of range, though as always, real-world mileage will depend heavily on rider weight, terrain, and how enthusiastically that throttle gets used.

Suspension duties are handled by an 80 mm dual-crown front fork, paired with 20×4-inch fat tires and hydraulic disc brakes with 180 mm rotors.

The bike also borrows several features more commonly associated with motorcycles, including traction control, hill-start assist, regenerative hill descent control, and automatic lighting.

Whether or not an e-bike requires traction control or hill hold remains to be seen, but it’s neat to know that such moto-inspired tech is heading into the e-bike space.

Segway continues to lean heavily into connected features as well. The Xyber Air includes AirLock automatic unlocking, Apple Find My compatibility, GPS tracking, Lost Mode remote disabling, over-the-air updates, and a full-color TFT display with navigation and smartphone integration.

Some connected services will require a subscription after the first year, which is unfortunately becoming a trend in the micromobility world, but makes sense given the data connection required for those services. Still, it’d be nice to see more of a grace period, like two to three years, for connected features, since it’s not like we’re downloading gigabyte-heavy movies on our bikes.

Despite all of those features, components, and tech, the Xyber Air weighs a claimed 84 lb (38 kg), which is noticeably lighter than the original Xyber, while still supporting a 330 lb (150 kg) payload. It’s also UL 2271 and UL 2849 certified.

Sure, 84 pounds is a lot of poundage for an e-bike, but compared to the moto-styled original, it’s on a significant diet.

Ordering will open on October 27 at a launch price of $1,999, though customers can already sign up on the sales page to get availability notifications.

I actually think Segway made the right move here.

The original Xyber had that cool flair to it, but it also blurred the line between e-bike and electric motorcycle, or shot right past it in many places. The Xyber Air looks like Segway took a step back and asked, “What if we kept the styling that people liked but made it fit within the existing e-bike framework?”

Basically, they kept the “Let’s take a shot at SUPER73” mindset but aimed for a more acceptable format considering today’s regulatory landscape.

The result is still unmistakably moto-inspired, but it’s also something that can legally access bike infrastructure in many places instead of existing in a regulatory gray area. At under $2,000, it also lands at a price point that opens the door to a larger audience.

It’s still not going to compete against the value proposition in something like the Juiced Scrambler, either in hardtail or full-suspension format, but it definitely looks like a fun ride. And with more options for more riders, there’s always going to be something for everyone!

#4863. What You Should Know About Exercising When Bone Density Is a Concern

Osteopenia or osteoporosis doesn’t have to sideline your workouts. Here’s what to do, how to modify, and when to back off.

You might have heard that being active is a good idea when you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, conditions marked by lower-than-normal bone density. But when you’re exercising specifically to improve bone health, some types of exercise may be more helpful than others. Before lacing up your sneakers, there are a few things to know.

“When patients ask me what they can do to preserve and protect their bone health, consistent weight bearing and resistance exercises are the first things I recommend,” says Nicole Leung, MD, director of the Osteoporosis and Bone Health Program at NYU Langone Health in New York City. “Bone is a living tissue, so it adapts to mechanical load through remodeling.”

When bone tissue is stressed via physical activity, your body responds by making more bone, helping strengthen the tissue. Exercise also lowers the activity of cells that dissolve and break down old bone. That combo helps preserve or even improve your bone mineral density, regardless of your health status. Exercise may slow or even prevent the progression of osteoporosis; if you have osteoporosis already, it can help you maintain the bone you have and reduce your risk for falls and fractures.

A bone-density diagnosis doesn’t mean you have to give up exercise—but your routine should reflect your fracture risk and health history. Here’s what Dr. Leung recommends for choosing activities, adapting your routine, and knowing when to check with your doctor before making major changes.

There are a few types of activities that make up a bone-friendly exercise plan, and it’s important to get the right amount of each. Here are the types of exercise to do regularly.

These are exercises where you’re on your feet and putting force on your muscles and bones as they work against gravity. Depending on factors like your age, fitness level, and bone mineral density, these activities can include:

People working to maintain their bone health should do these sorts of activities for 30 to 60 minutes, three to five days per week, according to the American College of Sports Medicine.

As for activities like swimming and cycling, they’re great for getting your heart pumping—but because they’re low-impact, they won’t do much for your bones. That said, feel free to do them in addition to your weight-bearing exercises if you enjoy them.

Lifting (relatively) heavy things works your muscles and helps build bone density. This includes free weights, machines, resistance bands, or body weight exercises like squats or push-ups. Aim for two to three strength sessions per week, and don’t be afraid to gradually go heavier (with your doctor’s okay). Pushing yourself to 70 to 90 percent of your max effort may deliver a bigger bone boost than lifting lighter weights, research suggests.

Having osteoporosis makes you more prone to fractures after falls, but you can strengthen your balance—and reduce your chances for a broken bone—with exercises like yoga, tai chi, or Pilates. “Any exercise where you have to shift your body weight side to side and forward and back can be very helpful for your stabilizing muscles,” Dr. Leung says. She recommends working balance exercises into your schedule a few times per week. Find safe modifications if you’re worried about falling, like holding onto a sturdy chair or touching a wall.

Whether you’ve been exercising for years, are just starting out, or are returning to a routine after a long hiatus, Dr. Leung advises paying attention to your posture, avoiding exercise when you’re overly exhausted, and increasing intensity gradually. Older women who are new to exercise can still do resistance training, she says, but may need to start at a slower pace and under supervision.

Despite the overall benefits of exercise, you still need to be careful, particularly when you have osteoporosis. Certain activities can set the stage for potential spine fractures, so before starting an exercise program, decide with your doctor or other qualified professional what is and isn’t safe for you.

According to the International Osteoporosis Foundation, you may need to limit or avoid moves that involve:

Yoga, while helpful for balance, can involve poses that put your spine at risk (like forward bends, deep twists, plow pose, shoulder stand, and pigeon pose). If you decide to give it a try, choose a class where the teacher can offer safe modifications, Dr. Leung says. It’s also best to steer clear of activities that come with a high risk of falling from above standing height, like skiing or horseback riding, she adds.

When it comes to stressing your bones, it’s possible to get too much of a good thing. “Overburdening your bone can actually lead to stress fractures,” Dr. Leung says. If you do prolonged intense weight-bearing and high-impact exercises like jogging or jumping rope, avoid scheduling them on back-to-back days. Alternate those workouts with activities like strength training, or have an active recovery day where you walk or do yoga or tai chi, she recommends.

Make it a point to stay active even after you’ve completed the day’s workout. According to Dr. Leung, non-exercise activities like casual walking or doing chores may help to maintain bone density when compared to sedentary behavior. Stroll over to chat with a coworker at their desk during a break, take the stairs when you can, or walk while you call a friend instead of sitting. A few minutes here and there can really add up.

Any new or worsening bone or spine pain is a warning sign to stop exercising and contact your doctor. You should also call your doctor if you fall while exercising, notice that you’ve had height loss, or if your spine appears curved, which could be signs of a spinal fracture. And always stop exercising and seek medical attention if you experience other severe symptoms like dizziness, faintness, or chest pain.

Consistency counts. People with low bone density who stay active over several months tend to see the greatest bone-health benefits, studies show. Choose activities you enjoy, build up gradually, and find a rhythm you can sustain. The goal isn’t to nail every workout—it’s to keep movement in your life.

#4862. Jaylen Brown Is Keeping His Boston Skyrise Apartment—and Its 18th-Century Harp Too

Jaylen Brown has an 18th-century harp sitting in his living room, and that harp rules. Having a harp in your home as a newly 30-year-old man, with a professional harpist who appears when the mood strikes said 30-year-old man, is an outstanding use of free will.

“Most of the time I use my harp, it’s just me and my chef,” Brown says. A memory raced through my head: me at the end of my twenties, with a harp (broken) in my unit. And how central it would be to the social hours of 10 p.m. to 4 a.m.

Brown’s harp is not that. “It’s almost like therapy sessions,” he says.

Jaylen Brown with his cat Forky in the speakeasy of his Boston apartment design by Linda Zarifi of Zarifi Design. The project construction is by Core Group Boston, and the art advisory is by Miranda Girard. The sofa is by Charles Zana from The Invisible Collection and the ottoman is also from The Invisible Collection.

The artwork in the speakeasy is by Francisco Valverde and flanked with sconces by Apparatus. The curtain fabric is by Dedar, and the star ceiling lights are by UFO Lighting.

The wallcovering in the speakeasy is by Gregorius Pineo.

He’s a different dude in a way that makes him singular, both as a member of the National Basketball Association and as a young and famous Black man in the United States of America.

On July 1, 2026, hundreds of television talkers said “the basketball world has been turned upside down,” because Brown’s years as a Celtic were over. After nine years as half of Boston’s dynamic duo with Jayson Tatum, he was traded to Philadelphia. “It’s no beef,” Jaylen politely told reporters after a victory, beard absolutely glistening. “Might be a little lamb chops and gravy. He should stay ready at all times.” 23 days later, Brown’s new teammate became LeBron James, creating one of the strongest starting fives in NBA history. You love to see someone find a nice new gig. But as for where he rests his head, Brown held on to his place in Boston.

In the foyer, the walls are painted in Ashland Slate by Benjamin Moore. The custom table holds Brown’s championship trophy.

In the living area, the Hamilton sofa by Minotti surrounds coffee tables by Carlyle Collective. The floor lamp is by Tom Dixon and the harp is antique.

“I grew up here, age 19 to 29,” he says. “I developed here in Boston as a young man.” The feeling is mutual; October 24, his birthday, was named Jaylen Brown Day by the city. But the crib itself is doing a lot of the pulling. “There’s been other places, but this one–I created it, it was crafted by my vision,” he says. “This one felt the most like home.”

He hired a team to bring his dreams to life. Linda Zarifi, of Zarifi Design, was his interior designer and collaborator. “The first thing he said was ‘I don’t want a dining table,’” Zarifi says. “And I’m like, ‘Where are you going to…eat?’”

The answer was a 22-foot banquette, built for most home activities. “I wanted to open the space up. I wanted gold. I wanted a see-through wine cellar. She went and found it all,” Brown says.

The custom dining banquette is upholstered in Crescendo Suede by Kravet and the glass and metal tables are also custom by Jamie Cumming. The TG-10 Sling dining chairs are by Gratz Industries and the wall sconces are by Gubi. Inside the frame on the wall is a proclamation from the city of Boston for Jaylen Brown Day.

Brown in the dining 22-foot banquette playing chess.

The result is a 4,000 square-foot apartment overlooking Boston’s Financial District. Brown purchased the downtown space at the end of 2023 and reworked it over the last two years. Outside, the apartment is a brief 15 minute walk from the TD Garden, home to Brown’s former team, the Boston Celtics. Inside, Italian marble bathroom floors, 24-karat fixtures that Brown calls “jewelry for the bathroom,” a custom suede pool table, a party-ready speakeasy, and that see-through wine cellar.

There’s also the medical hyperbaric chamber one step from his bed, one of the truest signs that he is a single man.

Jaylen is figuring it out in real time, and he’s letting us watch and listen.

The trophy case in the speakeasy is a custom design by Zarifi and fabricated by Jamie Cumming of Loki Custom Furniture.

A shelf in the speakeasy holds a collection of Brown’s memorabilia.

A chandelier by John Pomp hangs over the bar area with stools by Blackman Cruz upholstered in a leather by Holly Hunt.

Kashmir barstools from Resident tuck under the kitchen counter. The flushmounts are from RH and the kitchen cabinets are painted in Cheating Heart by Benjamin Moore.

They say he’s not new to this. In 2020, five days after George Floyd was murdered, he drove 15 hours from Boston to our hometown of Atlanta to lead a march. The same guy who took the swooshes off his Nikes and now has his own shoe company (with custom closets by Molteni to house his own collection). And the same guy who uses this home to stream with Lil Baby and to display art and artifacts dedicated to his family.

“The things that he would splurge on are the things that mattered most to him,” Zarifi says. There’s the commissioned portrait in cracked glass by Simon Berger of his grandmother in the foyer. “For him, his flex was his harp.”

Brown seated on a bench in the primary bedroom. The custom bed is upholstered in a fabric by Mokum Textiles. The pendants by Apparatus hang over custom nightstands flanking the bed.

“I had them recreate the bedding and the comforter of the Four Seasons,” Brown says. The bedding is custom from Crem & Co. Brown’s hyperbaric chamber is beside the bed.

“I love the tempered glass,” Brown says. The closet design is the Glis Closet System by Molteni. The pendant light is by Henge.

The custom vanity in the primary bathroom is flanked with sconces by Articolo. The fittings are by Dornbracht.

The tub and counters are topped in a Pietra Grey stone and the ceiling is painted Ashland Slate by Benjamin Moore.

The Sally armchair in the primary bedroom is by Minotti and covered in Holly Hunt fabric.

He hasn’t taken lessons yet, good for no more than an impassioned glissando. What he does do, however, is soak in the sounds from Li Shan Tan, the principal harp for the New Haven Symphony Orchestra, who plucks from his palace. “From time to time, when she is not around, I go and I try to recreate some sounds.”

#4860. This Picture-Perfect Suburban Kitchen Is an Argument for Maxed-Out Storage, Smart Appliances, and Custom Furniture

The house had everything a young family could want: classic Georgian architecture, a picturesque setting in East Glenview, Illinois, and a neighborhood where kids rode bikes and Golden Retrievers lounged in the sunshine. For a Chicago couple with three young sons, it checked early every box. The kitchen, however, was another story. Its awkward layout, dated appliances, and surprisingly scant storage made it feel ill-equipped for the demands of a family of five.

Fortunately, the problem was one that could be solved. Elizabeth Smolcich, principal interior designer of Glenview-based firm Mason & Brass, saw its potential. “We knew we’d have to do a heavy lift to make the kitchen feel like ours,” says homeowner Marie Gould. “Elizabeth had a vision for it that made it much more functional and kid-friendly for our family.”

Kitchen layout before and after. A wider doorway improves the flow between kitchen and living room, while removal of a corner booth created room for a larger island and the potential for more seating.

Homeowner Marie Gould with her sons in the renovated kitchen

Smolcich started by widening the opening between the kitchen and living room just enough to let Gould easily eyeball what her boys, ages 7, 6 and 3, are up to while she’s cooking. And removing an awkwardly positioned corner booth, one that was too small to seat four comfortably but obtrusive enough to impede the 450-square-foot room’s flow, gave the designer enough space to expand and center a new kitchen island.

This island, topped with smoky quartzite, provides plenty of counter space for prepping meals or rolling out dough, and even has enough room for the boys to perch on when they want a close-up view of the action. Above the island, Smolcich installed schoolhouse-style fluted glass pendants, which the couple loved for their timeless appeal. The most significant addition came in the form of a custom banquette that looks built into the island but is actually a movable bench. The family slides this upholstered piece to one the side of their dining table, which can expand from 66 inches to 96 inches, when they're hosting a crowd. (They’re expecting more than 40 friends and family for Thanksgiving this year.)

This is family who loves to entertain, says the designer. A double oven, then, was a necessity, as was a serious range that allows Gould to sear a steak with restaurant-quality char. Gould discovered the ultimate time-saving mom hack with her smart SKS range, which features a rapid preheat function and can boil a pot of water for pasta in just 60 seconds. It has both an induction cooktop to prevent tiny hands from burns as well as four gas burners that satisfy even the pickiest of eaters.

Two ovens were a necessity for the homeowners' busy household. Brizo Rook faucets and Visual Comfort Parkington sconces, both in brass, warm up the space.

The designer flanked the stove with open shelving to keep oils and seasonings within easy reach. The dual gas and induction SKS range features Smart Knob technology.

“They’re big on texture,” says Gould of her family. “They love a sear and a proper crust, which is no problem with this.” (That said, she says she personally appreciates the range’s sous vide capability best, although the SKS Smart Knobs, with LED screens for each knob to monitor heat levels and time remaining, are a close second.)

Over the range Smolcich installed hidden, integrated built-in storage to hold Gould’s go-to oils and seasonings. “We took advantage of any and all real estate,” explains the designer. “We can make anything beautiful. That’s not the hard part of what we do. The hard part is making it wildly functional. If you feel like you have to go out of your way to retrieve something, you’re never going to love it.”

Designer Elizabeth Smolcich's mood board of furniture, lighting, and surfaces

Hence the dual SKS dishwashers staggered from the Kohler prep sink in the island to the main Kohler sink (with a custom cutting board!) on the perimeter; the pantry wall (painted Benjamin Moore Black Iron); an appliance garage (housing her toaster, blenders, mixer and coffee maker); and a beverage bar with a 24” second fridge stocked with her kids' juice boxes.

Prominently displayed is a treasured side-by-side picture frame with a photo of Gould’s parents baking with her oldest son next to a handwritten copy of their family's banana bread recipe.

“That’s what this kitchen is to them,” says Smolcich. “In a few years, those boys will be sitting at that banquette doing their homework. We took this big house with a kitchen built for just a few people and made it one for a family.”

The beverage bar includes an under-the-counter refrigerator where the kids can grab their juice boxes.

#4859. Why Real Paintings Can Look AI-Generated

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Take a look at the two moonlit scenes below. One was painted in 1839. The other was generated by artificial intelligence (AI) in 2026. Which one would you choose as being the work of a human artist?

Before looking for the answer, consider what guided your choice. The light? The details? Perhaps one looks a little too polished, while the other feels more natural. How confident are you that those qualities tell you who made it?

I find this question interesting because it asks us to examine something we might otherwise take for granted: what human creativity is supposed to look like.

In a preliminary, unpublished study, I asked 202 U.S. adults to judge images drawn from five 19th-century paintings and five AI-generated versions of the same scenes. Each participant saw five images, presented individually in random order, and identified each as human-made, AI-generated, or something they were unsure about.

Among the 920 answers that named a source, participants were correct about 45 percent of the time. For these images, that was below the 50 percent expected from a coin flip.

But the direction of the mistakes was more interesting. Participants labeled the original paintings as AI-generated 51 percent of the time. They gave that label to the actual AI images only 42 percent of the time. The original looked more artificial than its AI counterpart in four of the five pairs.

And the answer to the opening question? Image A is Johan Christian Dahl’s View of Dresden by Moonlight, painted in 1839. Image B is AI-generated. Among definite answers, 69 percent labeled Dahl’s painting AI, compared with 51 percent for the generated version.

This reversal has a parallel in poetry. Brian Porter and Edouard Machery found that nonexpert readers were more likely to attribute AI-generated poems to humans than poems actually written by established poets (2024). Our expectations about human expression can apparently lead us away from the humans.

Why might this happen? Participants’ explanations offered a clue. Nearly a quarter mentioned a polished or “too perfect” appearance as a sign of AI. That seems like a reasonable suspicion until we consider how much effort painters have devoted to achieving precisely those qualities.

Consider the still life below. The original is Image B, painted by Severin Roesen in 1852. Its elaborate arrangement and luminous fruit might fit someone’s idea of what an image generator produces. Yet here those qualities belong to a human painter.

One possible explanation is what psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman called the representativeness heuristic: judging something by how closely it resembles our idea of a category (1974). If our mental picture of AI art is smooth, detailed, and beautifully lit, a painting with those features may seem machine-made. (This is an interpretation of the findings; the study did not experimentally establish that polish caused the mistakes.)

Experience offered little reassurance. Regular users of AI image tools were less likely to answer “not sure,” but showed no detectable accuracy advantage. Being comfortable making a judgment and being correct about it are separate matters.

Of course, five painting pairs cannot tell us how people judge all art. Participants viewed digital reproductions, and each made only five judgments. The results do not establish that expertise is useless or that nobody can detect AI. They do suggest that familiar visual clues can mislead us in this particular setting.

That matters because authorship can change appreciation. In experiments by Lucas Bellaiche and colleagues, artworks received more favorable evaluations when labeled human-created rather than AI-created, even though all the images were generated by AI (2023). The story we attach to an image can become part of what we see in it.

What gives me pause is the possibility that we might dismiss human skill precisely because it looks accomplished. Before treating an image as obviously artificial, I would want to know more about where it came from.

Dahl painted that moonlit scene in 1839. The suspicion that it looks like AI belongs entirely to us.

Porter, B., & Machery, E. (2024). AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably. Scientific Reports, 14, 26133. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76900-1

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

Bellaiche, L., Shahi, R., Turpin, M. H., Ragnhildstveit, A., Sprockett, S., Barr, N., Christensen, A., & Seli, P. (2023). Humans versus AI: Whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-023-00499-6

#4858. Erin and Sara Foster Reveal the Rule That Keeps Their Business—and Sisterhood—Working

The Nobody Wants This producers stop by the latest episode of The Huddle.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’ve binged all three seasons of the Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, presided over a board meeting in your chicest Favorite Daughter blazer, or nodded along to a cringey dating anecdote while listening to The World’s First Podcast, you are no doubt familiar with the work of multi-hyphenate sisters Erin and Sara Foster.

Raised in Los Angeles (dad is famous record producer David Foster), the sisters first gained notoriety with their VH1 mockumentary series, Barely Famous, in 2015. Since then, they’ve gone on to launch several successful businesses, including their clothing line and a production company, Fatigue Sisters Productions. (They even recently served as guest sharks on ABC’s Shark Tank.)

With the season 3 premiere of Nobody Wants This (based on Erin’s own experience of dating and marrying a Jewish man and later converting to Judaism), the dynamic duo stopped by the Women’s Health podcast The Huddle to chat with editors Abby Cuffey and Jacqueline Andriakos about doing business together, setting boundaries, and raising kids.

Erin and Sara launched their clothing line, Favorite Daughter, in late 2020 to fill gaps in their own closets. But as the company has grown and evolved over time, they’ve learned to put their customers at the heart of everything they do. It’s also forced the sisters to staff up with people who are willing to share their true opinions, rather than simply being yes-men or yes-women.

“That's something that is really challenging when you have a talent-focused brand,” Erin says. “It's taken a very long time for us to convince the people who work for us to be honest with us. That’s how people become monsters—no one's telling them the truth.”

“I always say, too, this is a democracy,” Sara adds. “This only works if everyone feels heard. This only works if you're allowed to do the thing that you're hired to do.”

Having a valued third or even fourth opinion also comes in handy when the two can’t see eye-to-eye, which happened often when the brand first launched.

“We’re in a good place today, but we would have blow-up screaming fights in fittings for many years at Favorite Daughter,” Erin says. “It’s tricky for us, because we do not have differentiated, carved-out roles. We have the exact same role, so if we disagree, it's really challenging to find the happy medium.”

In 2021, the sisters’ working relationship expanded further when they launched their podcast The World's First Podcast with Erin & Sara Foster. While the duo aren’t shy about diving into personal topics—be it romantic relationships or raising children—they have set certain boundaries to ensure their friends and family don’t end up embarrassed or as headline fodder.

“I have an idea of where [my husband’s] boundaries are,” Erin says. “He's not really into me talking about exes or other relationships.”

Sara, on the other hand, learned the hard way where one of her daughter’s boundaries lie when she revealed her juvenile arthritis diagnosis—in the hopes of helping other parents—and it was picked up by multiple outlets.

“It never occurred to me that that could happen,” Sara says. “My daughter was like, ‘I do not appreciate that.’ I was like, ‘Oh god, I'm so sorry.’”

Given that they have creative control over the podcast’s content, Erin and Sara do occasionally edit out portions that they think could be taken out of context with the TikTok-ification of media nowadays. “We try to err on the side of keeping things in, but then there's some times that you get a little ahead of yourself,” Erin says.

Speaking of raising daughters, Sara’s got even more wisdom to share on parenting—specifically about telling your kids the harsh truths about yourself.

“Being a mother is just such a exercise in getting humbled,” she says. “My instinct was always like, don't reveal yourself too much. Don't let them see your flaws. Don't tell them about all the times you f---ed up as a teenager yourself. But that's the opposite. You're really supposed to. Maybe some people disagree with this, but as they get older, you’re supposed to reveal mistakes you made, things that you wish you did differently... That has changed the dynamic with me and my older daughter—being honest with her about things that I wish I had done differently.”

Erin agrees: “I think it's probably better for your children to grow up knowing that you are a complicated, flawed person, and then you don't have to fall off a pedestal for them.”

To hear more from the sisters about how they find the creativity to create, their stance on kids and social media, and why they’re obsessed with a certain protein powder, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above!

#4856. I’m Running the New York City Marathon Topless. The Reason Is Not What You Think.

It was my 18-mile long run, the farthest I'd gone so far in my New York City Marathon training, when I felt anxiety creep into my ankles. Central Park was full of life and happiness, but I was suddenly acutely aware of every mile, every ache, and every vulnerability I couldn't outrun. “I could just stop right now,” I thought.

A year earlier, I was in active treatment for breast cancer at 32. I had undergone chemotherapy, a mastectomy, and reconstruction, and was still learning to recognize my new body. Now, I was preparing to run 26.2 miles, completely topless, with my scars visible.

But I pushed through the fear: This was exactly why I chose to run in the first place. Not because I’ve overcome everything or that I have nothing left to hide—but because I’m learning to show up as I am: Uncomfortable, imperfect, and still moving forward. I’m running like this in the hopes that my story might help save another woman’s life. If seeing me and learning about my journey helps her speak up or look into her own breast cancer risk, this run becomes bigger than me.

In 2023, I left my career as an associate in wealth management at Merrill Lynch to raise my son. Six short months after I resigned, everything changed.

I found a lump. My ob-gyn told me I was too young for a mammogram. An ultrasound came back benign. It was a third doctor, a breast surgeon, who finally took me seriously and sent me for a mammogram, a biopsy, and an MRI. She saved my life.

I was leaving the gym on an ordinary Thursday when the call came. I had breast cancer in both breasts: stage 2 triple-negative cancer on one side and stage 1 ER/PR-positive cancer on the other.

The world went blurry, and every sound was muffled. Was I dying? My son was only one. I couldn't leave him without a mother, and my husband without his partner. I had so much more life to live, and so much more to do. How had the first two appointments missed this?

My husband, Elio, and I built my care team at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and together we mapped out a plan: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and surgeries. Each decision I made along the way helped me feel a little more in control.

One of the hardest parts of treatment was confronting how much my body had changed. When I finally had my mastectomy, I braced myself to be horrified when the bandages came off. I shed one tear. It hit me that things would never be the same and that a part of my body I'd tied to my femininity and sexuality had been changed forever. I faced a choice no woman should have to make. For me, it was this or facing my mortality.

But the moment that still gets me isn't the one in front of the mirror. It was the afternoon my then-two-year-old son caught a glimpse of my chest.

"Mommy, you have a boo boo?” He asked. “Are you hurt? Do you need to go to the hosminal?"

I had tried to protect my son from knowing what I was going through—no two-year-old should have to learn what cancer is before they learn the alphabet. But still, he could tell something was wrong. I was proud of his sympathy and awareness, but at the same time, I was heartbroken he noticed. I dreaded telling him about my cancer diagnosis—especially given my BRCA diagnosis and the unknowns about whether I had passed it along to him.

Later, changing in a gym locker room for the first time since surgery, I flinched, covering my chest as I pulled off my sports bra. I never would have done that before cancer. Was I ashamed of the scars? Nervous that I looked different? Probably a bit of both. I gave myself grace for that instinctive reaction, but also promised myself then that I would no longer let shame drive how I felt about my body. My scars are evidence that I lived. They stand for tenacity, resilience, and bravery—traits I want my son to have and how I want him to remember me.

During treatment, I set a goal to run my first half marathon a few months after my mastectomy. It kept me focused and gave me something to look forward to, something beyond appointments, medications, and the uncertainty of treatment. Crossing the finish line felt powerful. I thought of all the work that I’d put in to get there and the many training sessions where I chose to show up for myself every day.

But shortly after, I was disappointed to learn I would need to continue oral chemotherapy to help reduce the risk of recurrence. This pushed my recovery timeline back and meant I’d have to wait longer for my reconstructive surgeries. So I set another goal: if I could run 13.1 miles, I could run 26.2 the following year, when I’d be done with treatment and surgeries.

I decided I would also run topless, putting on display the very thing I vowed to never hide. No shirt, no bra. To prevent chafing and provide makeshift support, I plan on using special styling tape donated by NOOD.

I would do it for the women who might have questions they want to ask their doctors, who feel like something isn’t right but keep minimizing their concerns. And I would also do it for the other survivors out there. I hope that by seeing me run, they also feel more comfortable in their bodies, scars and all.

I set my sights on the New York City Marathon, running with Fred’s Team, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center’s charity partner. I even created a subteam, Team Laklak, named after the beauty brand I co-founded during my cancer journey, offering science-based makeup that’s still full of color and fun. I’m proud that we’ve raised $45,000 to date for the very hospital that saved my life. It feels like such a full-circle moment that the beauty company I dreamed up while sitting in treatment chairs there can now give back to other women in this way.

I’m not the first woman to run a marathon topless, but I will be the first in New York City. In 2024, Louise Butcher also ran the London Marathon, showing off the scars from her mastectomy and flat closure reconstruction for similar reasons. I chose to reconstruct with implants—and I’m not sure if people will find my run more taboo or sexualized because of it. They shouldn’t. Louise and I faced the same disease and underwent similar treatments.

On November 1, I'll finish my 26.2 miles back in Central Park, the same park where I once thought, “I could just stop right now.”

My story is about more than learning to embrace my body after cancer. It's also about what can happen when women are dismissed, when they question their instincts, or when they assume they are too young to be at risk.

Breast cancer doesn't discriminate by age. Approximately one in eight women in the United States will be diagnosed in their lifetime, and a diagnosis can happen well before the age many women associate with routine screening. I was fortunate to find a breast surgeon who listened to me and pursued further testing, but not every woman knows what questions to ask or where to turn when something doesn't feel right. A breast cancer risk assessment tool can be a useful place to start. While it cannot diagnose cancer or replace medical advice from a physician, it can help women better understand their personal risk and discuss whether additional evaluation or screening may be appropriate.

Whether we're navigating cancer or chasing a marathon finish line, we will all have moments when we want to stop. We may not feel fearless or ready. We may not know exactly what comes next. But we can take the next step, ask the next question, and learn to trust ourselves along the way.

I'm running topless because I no longer want to hide my scars. I'm running because I'm still here and because I can. But most of all, I'm doing this in the hope that another woman will feel a little more empowered to take charge of her own story.

Lauren Spiezia is a breast cancer survivor who carries the BRCA2 mutation and the founder of Laklak Beauty, a clean cosmetic brand built from her experience as an oncology patient. More at laklakbeauty.com/run.

#4853. LiveWire set to show off several new electric motorcycles next month

LiveWire is preparing to bring its biggest electric two-wheeler lineup yet to EICMA (Milan Motorcycle Show) next month, including a pair of previously unseen models that will offer a preview of where the electric motorcycle company is headed in 2027.

The company will exhibit alongside its majority shareholder Harley-Davidson at the massive Milan motorcycle show, running November 5-8, where its booth will span everything from STACYC electric balance bikes to the lightweight S4 Honcho platform and the more performance-oriented DUST family.

Perhaps the biggest surprise will be the first public appearance of the new S4 Honcho Skate. LiveWire hasn’t revealed much about the bike yet, other than confirming it will expand the Honcho family when it arrives in 2027. We won’t have to wait until EICMA for all the details, though, as LiveWire says preliminary specs and additional information will be released on November 2.

The Skate will join the S4 Honcho Street and S4 Honcho Trail, giving LiveWire a growing family of lightweight electric motorcycles built around its modular S4 platform. The production-ready Honcho Street will also make its European debut at EICMA before going on sale there immediately after the show. Its U.S. launch is scheduled for next week.

LiveWire is also continuing to flesh out its newly acquired DUST lineup. After acquiring the assets of Dust Moto earlier this year, LiveWire will show off a production-intent version of the DUST Hightail, which is targeting a 2027 introduction.

We are rewatching the classic series Babylon 5. Yesterday we saw the episode where the B-Plot was Garabaldi rebuilding a 1995 Kawasaki Ninja 1100. Lennier offers to help and mentions that 'the last gasoline powered motorcycle was built in 2035'.

We may not be that far off of the timeline.

(When I first saw the show 2035 seemed so far away LOL)

Alongside it will be another new model known as the DUST Spur, also planned for 2027. Like the Honcho Skate, details remain thin for now, with preliminary specifications coming November 2 and final production specs and pricing expected in the first quarter of next year.

The expanding lineup is particularly interesting because it shows just how far LiveWire is moving beyond the premium full-size electric motorcycles that defined the brand’s early years.

Between STACYC, the lightweight Honcho models, and the more dirt-focused DUST machines, LiveWire is increasingly building a ladder of electric two-wheelers aimed at riders across a much wider range of ages, experience levels, and budgets.

We’ll get a much better look at the newest rungs on that ladder in just a couple of weeks.

#4852. Why Fighting Against Social Anxiety Could Be Making It Worse

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

When we feel ourselves getting socially anxious, our knee-jerk reaction is often to try to avoid it. But if we welcome it in, the effect can be quite different from what we expect.

Most people have felt socially anxious at one time or another. Think about what’s going through your mind before giving a speech, during an important job interview, or, really, any situation where you worry about what others might think of you.

In addition to—and indeed connected to—these in-the-moment thoughts, there are physical sensations: butterflies in the stomach, trembling, or a dry mouth, to name but a few. When I interviewed socially anxious women as part of my research (Masters, 2024), many spoke about blushing and sweating (Farah*), while others described feeling nauseous (Daniella).

It might be tempting to think of social anxiety as having mental and physical aspects, and it’s likely so difficult to get away from this because we don’t really have a word—in common usage, at least—that conveys that we’re talking about the whole self.

Yet, thinking about the mental and the physical as existing independently might not be that helpful (despite what mind-body dualist philosopher Descartes would have us believe!), especially in this context. Another woman I interviewed, Amy, was herself pretty critical of the notion that the mind and body are distinct, calling it "a fallacy." Instead, Amy advocated for a more integrated or biopsychosocial view. An article by the Royal College of Psychiatrists (2016) explains this rather nicely in the case of social anxiety—that is, how emotions affect the body, and vice versa:

"Other people may be able to see some of the signs of this anxiety—the blushing, stammering, shaking and trembling.

These symptoms can be quite alarming and make your anxiety worse. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

You worry so much about looking worried that you actually do look worried."

What we have here is a feedback loop being set up: You worry about what others think of you; you exhibit some of the physical signs of social anxiety; you then worry that others can see these signs and they’ll think badly of you; the social anxiety becomes worse; the physical symptoms are exacerbated; and so on.

The key to breaking this feedback loop could lie, counterintuitively, not in trying to prevent these physical manifestations, but in doing the opposite: embracing them. By way of example, those among you who are prone to blushing: Has there ever been a time when you’ve successfully managed to stop blushing simply by willing your cheeks to be less red, or trying really, really hard not to? Or have these strategies instead made the blushing worse?

The idea of turning toward, instead of turning away from, difficult sensations or emotions has its roots in some branches of meditation or mindfulness. I first came across this as part of my own journey in working through the book Overcoming Worry and Generalised Anxiety Disorder a few years ago. In the appendices, psychologists Mark Freeston and Kevin Meares signpost the reader to mindfulness, in particular citing Jon Kabat-Zinn and Mark Williams as names the reader might want to look up.

One of the key tenets of mindfulness is acceptance: that is, letting go of the tendency that we have to want things to be different from how they are. Alongside this, Jon Kabat-Zinn (2023) often advocates putting out the welcome mat for, or letting in, difficult experiences, such as emotional distress or physical pain.

Freeston and Meares themselves espouse a strategy akin to this in their book on generalised anxiety disorder, wherein they suggest the reader writes down their worries and sets aside some time later in their day especially to "have a good worry." The thinking here is that, with the attention lasered in on the worry, the worry dissolves: a bit like looking under your bed and seeing the proverbial monster—it’s far less scary than you thought when viewed head-on instead of catching mere glimpses of it.

Applying this to social anxiety, let’s say you become embarrassed. Your default reaction might be, "Oh no, I’m blushing and sweating, and my voice is trembling." Then you start to worry that people notice, which makes it (the blushing et al.) worse, and so forth—exactly as we saw in the Royal College of Psychiatrists’ article.

So how do we break this feedback loop? An alternative to resisting or bracing against these experiences could lie in embracing them, or welcoming them in. Next time you feel yourself becoming socially anxious, what happens if you lean into it—to whatever extent you’re comfortable doing so—and are curious about it? What are the sensations like? Exactly where are they? What qualities (shape/texture/temperature) do they have? What are the thoughts? Are they coming and going? How are they making themselves known? And how is all of this changing with time?

Following Freeston and Meares, what we’re doing here could be described not as letting ourselves "have a good worry," but as letting ourselves "have a good old experience of social anxiety." And while we may not be able to rid ourselves completely of the social anxiety itself (and all of its associated physical sensations)—at least not right away—letting it be there, instead of pushing it away, can be a very different, and perhaps less distressing, experience. As Kabat-Zinn (2019) has written in relation to dealing with life's difficulties: "You can’t stop the waves, but you can learn to surf."

* Names have been changed to protect anonymity

Freeston, Mark, and Kevin Meares (2015). Overcoming Worry and Generalised Anxiety Disorder: A Self-help Guide Using Cognitive Behavioural Techniques (2nd edn.) Robinson: London.

Kabat-Zinn, Jon (2023). Mindfulness Meditation for Pain Relief: Practices to Reclaim Your Body and Your Life. Sounds True: Colorado, US.

Kabat-Zinn, Jon (2019). Wherever You Go, There You Are: Mindfulness Meditation for Everyday Life. London: Piatkus.

Masters, Katie (2024). Feminist and Anti-psychiatry Perspectives on ‘Social Anxiety Disorder’: The Socially Anxious Woman. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan

Royal College of Psychiatrists (2016). Shyness and Social Phobia

#4849. Construction Carnaval: electric equipment comes to Brazil with SDLG

SDLG Brasil has completed its first sale in the South American country, delivering an order of six heavy-duty electric wheel loaders to Brazilian mining, construction, and infrastructure company Grupo Base.

Grupo Base ordered four, 27-ton L972 HEV and a pair of, 12.5-ton L938 HEV loaders from Chinese equipment brand Shandong Lingong Construction Machinery Co., Ltd. (the “SD” is “ShanDong,” the LG is “LinGong”) back in June, and the first of the machines are now reportedly on-site, moving dirt, but not making noise.

“This contract is a historic milestone and comes at a time when we have taken on commercial responsibility for SDLG across 60% of Brazil,” says Carlos Renato Machado, executive director of SDLG’s Brazilian distributor, Tracbel, before adding that the company hoped to expand the use of electric mining and construction equipment throughout the region.

The SDLG machines draw power from 423 and 180 kWh LFP battery packs, respectively, with the larger machines sending power to a 230 kW (~305 hp) electric motor and the smaller machines getting a 180 kW (~240 hp) one. Both specs promise a full day’s worth of continuous operation and fast DC charging between shifts.

Grupo Base operates a fleet of 450 heavy equipment assets at more than 30 concrete and mortar batching plants and 20 crushed stone and fracking sand sites, employing more 2,000 people. The electrification of those assets would represent a massive environmental benefit to the ecologically sensitive region – and that’s a fact not lost on Grupo Base executives.

“We are driving a major transformation across our operations,” says Edson Pechio, president and CEO of Grupo Base, said. “We want to incorporate solutions that will enable us to operate more efficiently and progressively reduce greenhouse gas emissions.”

#4848. Volkswagen recalls nearly 73,000 EVs due to faulty batteries

Volkswagen issued a recall affecting nearly 73,000 EVs globally. Until a remedy is available, VW will limit charging on impacted vehicles to 80% of their maximum battery capacity.

After issuing a recall with the NHTSA earlier this month that impacts 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs in the US, official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) reveals several thousand more EVs are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, a total of 72,668 EVs are impacted worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

Volkswagen issued the recall after an internal investigation found that some battery cells produced during that period do not meet specifications. The recall stems from a supplier defect.

In some instances, “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation,” or a battery fire, Volkswagen said.

Until a remedy is available, Volkswagen is urging owners to limit charging to 80% of its max capacity. If technically possible, VW said: “the maximum available charging capacity will be temporarily limited to 80% by the system.”

In the US, Volkswagen emailed owners of vehicles included in the recall, saying that unless they opt out by October 21, it “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%.”

The update will be done remotely and reflected in the mobile app on or about October 27, 2026. Some owners have already received the update.

Sounds like VW's "GM Bolt" moment. Sad. This is a huge cost due to a supplier's failure (but fully understandable and needed), not to mention owners frustration with EVs and the brand.

Volkswagen is still working on a remedy. Letters informing owners of the risks are expected to be mailed out on November 27, 2026. Once the remedy is available, VW will send additional letters.

Owners can contact Volkswagen’s customer service at 1-800-893-5298 with questions or concerns. VW’s recall number is 93EX.

Those in the US can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit NHTSA.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V630.

The manufacturer’s recall codes with the German KBA are 93MV, 93MF, and 93W4 (for the Cupra Born).

#4846. 5 Reasons to Fall in Love with La Quinta

Whether you’re visiting to play, explore, or simply chill, this desert paradise in California’s Coachella Valley has a little something for everyone.

Every day, from deciding whether or not to hit snooze to choosing to read a few more pages before shutting our eyes, our brains are a blur of choices—approximately 35,000 according to prevailing research. And frankly, it’s exhausting trying to make the right one every time. A vacation reboot would help… but travel planning requires even more decisions, which obviously defeats the purpose. And so the trip gets backburnered again.

What if there was a place that made choosing easy—because there’s no possible wrong answer? A land where you could decide to do all the things on the visitor’s bureau checklist, or none of them, and have an equally good time?

Enter La Quinta, California, a city of championship golf courses, towering palms, sprawling resorts with pools and spas, Old Hollywood lore, dramatic mountain backdrops, purple skies at dusk, and savory restaurants tucked into a calm corner of the Coachella Valley. It’s a place where you’re encouraged to do only what you love and what makes you feel most alive. Here in this sun-kissed slice of paradise, choose to follow the itinerary that is most Quinta-ssentially you.

There are 20 golf courses within the city limits, including the nine at the PGA West, a 2,000-acre luxury golf resort and community. Among those are the Mountain Course and the Stadium Course, which blend stunning natural beauty, manicured landscapes, challenging holes and expert designs by masters Pete Dye, Jack Nicklaus, and Greg Norman.

You can hit up the pickleball and tennis courts at Fritz Burns Park from dawn until well past dusk. The 12-acre green space also features a skate park, a children’s playground, a pool, and a dedicated area to play fetch with your pup. If you need to brush up on the rules of your chosen game, book some time with the pros at La Quinta Resort & Club, where you can rent equipment or pick up a match.

Whether you’re craving laid-back brunch bites, like the huckleberry hotcakes or double smashburgers at the farm-to-table eatery Beautiful Day, or a night on the town enjoying minty lamb chops and mai tais exploding with citrusy pucker at DSRT Club, La Quinta’s culinary scene does not disappoint.

Greet the day with Mexican delicacies like machaca or chilaquiles on the colorful porch at Casa Mendoza. If you have a hankering for south-of-the-border specialties later in the day, they also make a mean molcajete, seafood enchiladas, or tacos al pastor. Come afternoon, head to La Quinta Cliffhouse for the legendary nightly happy hour and stay for supper at sunset. There, you can put the date in date night by snacking on Medjools with bacon, blue cheese, coconut, and honey. (Pro tip: always order the gooey stone fruit however it’s served, whether as a shake, syrup or side dish—the Coachella Valley grows 95% of the dates in the U.S.) Close out the night with a slice of decadent Toll House Pie, a fixture at The Sandbar for four decades.

Those who believe it is just as important to nourish the mind as it is the body can take a walk down memory lane at the free La Quinta Museum, where the newly expanded history and culture exhibit details the people, technologies, and businesses that shaped the city, including the Cahuilla Indians, homesteaders, the railroad, and the celebrity magnet La Quinta Resort, which is celebrating its centennial this year. At the museum, visual learners can study the massive mural and a collection of photographs.

La Quinta itself is a patron of the arts. It’s hard to miss the more than 160 sculptures, murals, and decorated utility boxes installed through the Art In Public Places program. Twice a year, creatives from around the world descend on the civic center campus and turn it into a concert venue and an alfresco art gallery for a four-day festival. After admiring the artwork, head over to Old Town for locally made mementos. The charming retail district—known for its pleasing Spanish colonial architecture and vibrant sprays of bougainvillea—stocks gems at independent boutiques and galleries year-round and hosts the open-air Art on Main Street event on select Saturdays from November to April.

The area is a bonanza for outdoor activity. Bike along the base of the Santa Rosa Mountains using the paved, 2.7-mile-long Bear Creek Trail, or fix your attitude by gaining altitude on the miles of trails littered throughout the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto mountain ranges.

One popular route takes hikers a little more than six miles from the La Quinta Cove neighborhood to Lake Cahuilla, which is particularly peaceful at dawn or dusk. (The luckiest trekkers spy bighorn sheep.) Go straight to the lake to picnic, go horseback riding, or fish. Prolong your city escape by pitching a tent and camping at Cahuilla. Sunrise yoga and movie screenings are also offered lakeside.

While it’s clear there’s lots to do, know that, in the LQ, doing nothing is always on the table. Downtime happens to be a desert specialty, as there’s always a cold pool, a chaise lounge, and an umbrella drink calling your name. In fact, La Quinta Resort & Club boasts 42 pools across the 45-acre property, including a family-friendly splash zone and a more serene adults-only plunge with private cabanas and movie nights. (Don’t forget the 53 hot tubs for crisp Coachella nights.) Those who enjoy night swimming should post up at the never-closed pool at The Chateau at Lake La Quinta.

Finish the evening with stargazing and a glass of something sparkling in front of the fire pits. To really lean into relaxation, melt into a hot stone massage at Coral Spa or happily drift off while indulging in chromotherapy, a steam bath, or a dreamy scalp rub at Spa La Quinta. Or tap into an even deeper state of zen by joining a meditation or breathwork session or Sound Bath Sundays at Gather Yoga in Old Town. Plan your easiest trip ever today.

#4845. Lexus announces prices for its first 3-row electric SUV in Europe and the US

Lexus announced prices for its first fully electric three-row SUV, the 2027 TZ, with sales set to begin in the US later this year and in Europe in early 2027.

The new TZ is the largest, most luxurious Lexus electric SUV to date. It will go on sale by the end of 2026 in the US, and early 2027 in Europe.

In the US, the 2027 Lexus TZ will be available in three trims, starting at $64,050. The base TZ 450e Premium AWD model will be available to order in late 2026, followed by the Premium Touring AWD and Luxury AWD trims in early 2027.

The three-row electric SUV will be available with two battery packs: 76.96 kWh and 95.82 kWh. The former provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 253 miles, while the latter gets up to 315 miles.

#4844. Why Banning Social Media Won't Fix Teen Mental Health

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Imagine this. Nearly every teen in Teentown hangs out at the same place: the Teentown Pool. It’s the place to connect, meet new people, learn about parties, and unwind. There’s just one catch: There’s no lifeguard on duty. One exists, technically, but they’re not by the pool and respond to emergencies unreliably.

Despite this, management still encourages teens to swim as long as possible, even if they show signs of fatigue or hypothermia. Most swimmers are fine. But those who aren’t are told it's their own—or their family’s—responsibility to know when to get out of the pool, and to live with whatever anxiety, shame, or fear the experience leaves behind.

There’s another catch. The pool looks private, but it isn’t. Management films swimmers, profiles them, and sells their data to advertisers pushing products that may harm their health: diet supplements to teen girls with normal BMIs, steroids to teen boys. And though Teentown Pool is advertised as teen-safe, adults occasionally slip in, posing as teens, to engage in disturbing, even illegal behavior.

Teens do their best to manage these risks: reporting hazards, taking breaks, ignoring ads, and avoiding the creeps, but it’s unfair to ask them to do it alone. Even so, most teens keep coming back, because the alternative—missing out on where their friends are—carries its own weight. They’re stuck in a bind: Stay away from Teentown Pool and be isolated, or swim and constantly watch their backs.

Does this mean pools are inherently unsafe for teens? Should they be banned until age 16, granted entry only after their birthday? Or is the problem not with the pool, but rather with the management?

By now, you’ve probably guessed that I’m not talking about a community pool. The example is farcical, but it tracks the very real risks and trade-offs teens face on social media every day.

On Instagram, nearly half of teens report receiving unsafe content or unwanted messages within the past month, and those who do report feelings of discomfort, sadness, and fear. “It made me feel sad and insecure,” one 13-year-old boy reported in a 2025 survey conducted by Design It for Us. “I really wanted Instagram to remove that account. But I see that they are still up, victimizing individuals.” A 14-year-old girl added, “It made me afraid to be female and Asian. I did not feel safe.”

Additionally, despite claims that Instagram encourages teens not to overuse the platform, 65 percent of teens report that they haven’t received a single reminder to log off in the past six months. And harmful advertising is common: 41 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the U.K. have seen ads for prescription-only weight loss drugs, and Black teens are more than twice as likely as white teens to be targeted by skin-lightening ads (46 percent vs. 24 percent), in a country that has significantly stricter regulations than the U.S.

And yet the picture isn’t only negative. For many teens, especially Brown, Black, and queer young people, these platforms are often where they find community that’s harder to come by offline. LGBTQ+ teens are more than three times as likely to rate online spaces as “very kind and very safe” as compared to in-person spaces. Significantly more Black young people (77 percent) rate social media as important for connecting with others who share their mental health concerns than their white peers (53 percent). This is the real double bind: The same feed that exposes a teen to hate speech might also be the only place they feel seen.

So what should we, as caring adults advocating for young people in our own lives, be pushing for to keep teens safe? One commonly advanced solution is age-related bans or restrictions on social media use. While simple and intuitively appealing, bans don’t work, according to growing evidence. In Australia, more than 85 percent of teens circumvented the nationwide ban within months. Age-verification requirements also enable Big Tech to collect more, not less, intrusive personal data from users. Most importantly, bans don’t address the root of the problem—the fundamental mismanagement of online spaces. Harms associated with social media don’t disappear when young people turn 16 or even 18. Over half of 18- to 22-year-olds continue to report encountering racist, sexist, and homophobic content online, and 53 percent report that they feel like they can’t control their use or end up using social media for a longer amount of time than they wanted to.

There are also underappreciated harms associated with banning teens from social media, especially for Black, Brown, and queer teens for whom these platforms often function as vital sources of connection and support that aren’t readily available offline. Cutting off access doesn’t make the underlying platforms safer; it just removes a coping resource from teens who rely on it most, rather than offering the safety improvements companies have chosen not to make.

Instead of bans, we need to push policymakers for clear, enforceable consumer protection laws that make everyone’s safety and well-being non‑negotiable. We also need to push tech companies to partner with teens to redesign platforms to support mental health and publicly report on progress. People of all ages deserve safe spaces, both online and in person, to congregate, share ideas and interests, express themselves, and unwind. The public will is there. Now we need policymakers to put public good over private profit.

#4842. Why Women Over 50 Should Add This Underrated Carry to Their Strength Routine

“Many people think core training means crunches or planks, but one of the most functional ways to strengthen the core is by learning to resist movement,” says personal trainer Alice Jordan.

Her go-to exercise for doing exactly that? The kettlebell suitcase carry.

“Holding a kettlebell in one hand and walking with good posture forces the deep abdominal muscles, obliques, and spinal stabilizers to work continuously to keep your body upright,” explains Jordan, who specializes in strength training during perimenopause.

“For women over 50, this is particularly valuable because it develops balance, posture and stability while also improving grip strength, which is an important marker of healthy aging,” notes Jordan.

Indeed, one landmark study published in The Lancet found that lower grip strength was consistently associated with a higher risk of early death—even after accounting for age, physical activity, smoking, body size, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, the researchers reported that grip strength predicted somebody’s risk of dying better than systolic blood pressure.

The single-arm kettlebell suitcase carry, adds Jordan, “also translates directly into everyday activities such as carrying shopping, lifting luggage, or playing with grandchildren, making it a highly functional exercise.”

Below, Jordan explains how to do the exercise effectively and safely.

“Aim to include the exercise 2-3 times per week as part of a strength training program. It’s particularly effective when performed after your main strength exercises or as part of your core training,” adds Jordan.

As for how heavy a weight you should use for this exercise, Jordan recommends “choosing a kettlebell that feels challenging while still allowing you to maintain perfect posture throughout the walk.”

“You should be able to resist leaning to one side, keep your shoulders level and your core engaged from start to finish,” she adds.

“As a general guide, beginners might start with around 15-20 lb, while those with more strength training experience may use 20-30 lb or heavier, depending on their ability.”
