#4840. Eating Disorder Recovery in the Age of GLP-1s

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

You're planning your birthday dinner and text the group for restaurant ideas. One friend writes back that she's excited to celebrate but doesn't care where you go, since she probably won't eat much now that she's on Zepbound. Another suggests somewhere with "lighter options" because she started Wegovy. Someone else jokes that you can all split an appetizer.

You've worked hard to be able to sit down to a full meal and enjoy it. Now you're bracing to be the odd one out at your own birthday. You feel irritated and hurt. A couple of these friends know your history, and you can't understand how they can talk on the thread about their medications and how little they eat. Then you notice a voice you rarely hear anymore. Your eating disorder voice is back for a moment, bringing a twinge of envy and the thought that it's not fair. You remind yourself how dark that part of your life was and how much the illness took from you.

Weight-loss medications have been around for decades. In an earlier post, I wrote about their history, including the amphetamine “rainbow pills” handed out at diet clinics in the 1960s and the fen-phen boom of the 1990s. The pattern has been remarkably familiar: A medication arrives with promises of making weight loss easier, enthusiasm grows, and widespread use eventually reveals risks or limitations that received less attention at first. By then, another medication may be on the horizon, offering renewed hope that the results will be different this time. Today, much of that enthusiasm surrounds GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While weight-loss advertisements have appeared in magazines, on billboards, and on television for decades, what feels different about this wave is the degree of visibility and accessibility. Now, you can open Instagram to look at a friend's vacation pictures and find yourself watching a video about GLP-1 medications. Telehealth companies and med spas advertise directly to consumers, often offering prescriptions after a brief online intake. Even when you aren't looking for weight-loss information, you may find it filling your social media feeds.

At the same time, more conversations are treating body size as a medical issue. “Obesity” is now referred to as a chronic disease, with the classification still based on BMI, a calculation basd only on height and weight that doesn't measure an individual's health. This shift reinforces the assumption that people in larger bodies need medical treatment to lose weight. With GLP-1 medications in the spotlight, weight loss is often presented as something you're expected to pursue for your health. If you're in recovery from an eating disorder, these messages can be difficult to question, especially when they come from healthcare providers or are presented as responsible health decisions.

Hearing about these medications from people you know can be even more difficult. A friend mentions how little she eats now or a family member says they're relieved to stop thinking about food. They may have no idea how that sounds when you've worked so hard to eat enough and respond to hunger. These conversations can stir up old fears about weight gain or leave you questioning what you've learned from your eating disorder treatment providers, particularly when the people around you seem convinced that losing weight has improved their lives.

People who take these medications often say they think less about food. They may mention forgetting meals or feeling full after a few bites. If you're in eating disorder recovery, this can sound very much like the way you once described your illness. It can be disorienting to hear the experience being discussed with relief and sometimes pride, even by those who were once concerned about your “diet” and weight loss.

Much of eating disorder recovery involves learning to notice even subtle signs of hunger and eat in response. This may take years to achieve after you've learned to ignore or distrust your body. A friend talking about hunger as a problem that medication has solved can bring back doubts about whether responding to hunger is really the right thing to do, or even necessary.

The popular idea of "food noise" adds to the strain. Those of us working in the eating disorder field are very familiar with this phenomenon because being consumed with thoughts about food is a natural response to deprivation, as documented in the Minnesota Starvation Experiment in the 1940s1. We also know that labeling food “bad” and treating it as off-limits contributes to this “food noise.” Calling those thoughts noise to be silenced echoes what the eating disorder always claimed: that wanting food is the problem and quieting the want is the cure.

In order to protect your eating disorder recovery, it's necessary to separate someone else's choice from your own. Their decision to take a medication says nothing about what your body needs. Your friend's prescription came out of a conversation about their body. Your recovery came from years of work on your own.

Weight-loss talk can start before you have time to think about how you want to respond. Having one sentence in your back pocket can make those moments easier: “I'm trying to focus less on my weight and pay more attention to my body. Can we talk about something else?” You do not owe the whole table your history. I would practice saying it aloud, since boundaries can be harder to find when you're caught off guard.

While it's impossible to completely shield yourself from GLP-1 weight-loss messaging unless you move to a deserted island, it's possible to limit how much of it you actually consume. On social media, you can mute or unfollow accounts that post injection updates and before-and-after photos. If lunch turns into a conversation about weight loss and you can't, or don't have the energy to, redirect it, give yourself permission to excuse yourself.

At home, you may not get a break from it. If your partner or parent is on a weight-loss medication, you might sit down to dinner and watch them push away a plate that's still half full. They may mention how little they can eat now. Even when they say nothing, you take it in while you're trying to stay with your own hunger and fullness and enjoy the meal, all of which you worked hard to reclaim from your eating disorder. That's why the conversation at home needs to be more direct. Ask them to keep dose talk and body commentary away from shared meals. I imagine most people who care about you want to help and haven't connected their experience to your recovery.

If you're working with an eating disorder therapist or dietitian, bring these encounters to them, including the envy. Feeling a pull toward appetite suppression, wanting to lose weight, or fearing weight gain doesn't mean you're relapsing. It is useful clinical information about where your recovery needs support, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. Your therapist or dietitian can help you sort through what came up and plan for the next shared meal.

You return to the group chat, and this time your eating disorder doesn't get to write the reply. You pick the restaurant you love and plan to order what you want. You tell the friends who know your history that all this weight-loss talk is hard for you, as you've worked too hard to find peace with food and your body, and ask them to leave it out when you're together. Either way, you get to sit at your own birthday dinner and eat a full meal.

#4839. Lucid’s 25,000 Bolt robotaxis will run on Nvidia’s self-driving software

Lucid’s European robotaxi deal now has a driver. Bolt announced today that its fleet of at least 25,000 autonomous Lucid vehicles will run Nvidia’s Alpamayo Stack self-driving software, starting with a data-collection program in Madrid in 2027.

That gives Lucid two robotaxi customers on two different autonomy systems: Nuro’s software for Uber’s Gravity robotaxis in the US, and now Nvidia’s for Bolt in Europe.

When Lucid and Bolt announced the 25,000-vehicle deal last month, nobody said who would write the driving software. The vehicles were to be built around Nvidia Hyperion, a reference design for compute and sensors, which isn’t a self-driving system on its own. Bolt said it would bring in autonomous-driving partners later.

It picked Nvidia again. Alpamayo Stack is Nvidia’s full-stack driving software, which the company describes as “reasoning AI” combined with classical perception and planning, running on Hyperion with its Halos safety tools on top. The two will tune the software for European driving, and Lucid is only the first automaker Bolt plans to put it in.

Madrid comes first, in 2027. The cars there won’t carry riders at the start. Their job is to collect real-world driving data so Bolt and Nvidia can develop and validate the software, and even that still needs regulatory approval. Germany and France are named as the next key markets.

Jevgeni Kabanov, Bolt’s president and head of autonomous driving, said the Region of Madrid is “pioneering a structured framework for commercial autonomous mobility.” On Lucid’s side, the work runs through Lucid Technologies. Its president, Kay Stepper, called the “launch of data collection next year” one of “the first steps” toward autonomous mobility in Europe.

Bolt didn’t say which Lucid model goes to Madrid.

The September deal was designed around Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform, the same platform whose first vehicle, the Cosmos, got pushed to 2027 in Lucid’s August operating reset, “most likely the second half.” If the purpose-built vehicle isn’t ready in time, Madrid’s first data-collection cars would have to be existing Gravity or Air vehicles.

There’s also no date for anyone riding without a driver. Data collection is step one.

Add up both programs and Lucid has a lot of robotaxis on order, at least on paper. Uber’s program with Lucid and Nuro now calls for at least 35,000 Gravity vehicles globally, up from Uber’s original commitment to 20,000. Bolt adds at least 25,000. That’s 60,000 vehicles.

For scale, Lucid delivered 15,841 vehicles in all of 2025 and 10,852 in the first nine months of 2026. Those robotaxi commitments equal almost four years of Lucid’s current deliveries.

So Bolt is a company, with the same name as the Chevy Bolt. That makes the headline look a little confusing.

The Uber program is further along, but it isn’t open to the public yet. Uber employees have been taking test rides in Gravity robotaxis in San Francisco since April, with a safety operator behind the wheel. The public Bay Area launch is still promised for 2026, with Houston to follow in mid-2027.

Bolt is also hedging. It runs a separate track with Pony.ai and Stellantis, which announced a pilot in Luxembourg in June, and it’s targeting 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform across Europe and the wider UNECE region by 2035.

As for Nvidia, it has spent years selling chips and sensor reference designs to automakers. With Alpamayo Stack, it’s now selling the driver too, which puts it up against Nuro, Waymo, and Tesla’s software.

#4838. They’ve Taken on Clayface, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Star Trek. But Can They Survive Each Other?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing are some of the busiest comic book writers in the business—and their deep, complex, and long-standing friendship and working relationship is the biggest reason why.

RELATIONSHIPS ARE HARD. Interpersonal dynamics of any sort require work to maintain—Ben Affleck took a lot of shit for saying his marriage was work, but he was right. A myriad of different factors can destabilize a dynamic between people at any given moment: ego, money, miscommunication, and on the list goes.

Unless you’re Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing.

The comic writing duo, collectively and colloquially known as “Hivemind,” have worked on major properties including, but certainly not limited to, Captain America, Guardians of the Galaxy, Star Trek, and Thunderbolts. That’s not to mention their creator-owned work, like the new horror comic, You’ll Never Leave This Place Alive, which is akin to Marvel’s Runaways meets M. Night Shyamalan’s The Village. And right now, their work on the 2022 one-shot Batman: One Bad Day: Clayface, is part of the DNA that makes up Clayface—the latest production from James Gunn’s DC Studios and the current #1 movie in America. These are the kinds of projects that most writers would kill to be a part of. And, at every step, this pair has done it together.

In a profession where it often feels like a Battle Royale-style competition to land a paid gig, how and why do these two decide to work together?

The answer dates back to 2005, when the pair met at the University of Southern California’s famed film school. Lanzing remembers being on his very first film set and passing by a sound guy, David Server, talking about the Avengers. After doubling back and clarifying if he was, indeed, talking about the comic, the pair hit it off. Not long after, Lanzing went over to Server’s place to hang out, where he met Kelly, who was Server’s roommate. “We met briefly and became friendly,” Lanzing says. “I was definitely—let’s say—a little more hubristic back then,” Kelly states. “I think I was a little bit high on my own supply and wasn’t really quite as engaging with other folks as much.” Kelly went off to Ireland to study abroad and “came back and discovered that this guy, [Lanzing], was still in our lives. I really thought it was going to be a short, summer fling.”

The trio would pile in a PT Cruiser lovingly nicknamed “The Beast,” because it would “growl anytime you tried to gas it” and trek down to local comic book shops Golden Apple or Meltdown to pick up new issues for the week. The trio would then go to a greasy pizza place, read their books, and talk about them. “Because we were all film students, we’re breaking apart the story,” Kelly says. “We were really doing our best to effectively just be passionate nerds within the space. Once you spend enough time with someone and see their real passion for something, it's hard not to start to bond. Once you start to see that passion in someone's eyes and understand what they care about, that's how real relationships are built.”

In a way, Kelly’s relationship with Server developed as a Step Brothers-esque “Did we just become best friends” moment. But his relationship with Lanzing had more of the slow-burn nature of a courting.

“It genuinely was,” Kelly confirms. “Absolutely.”

If hanging out and talking shop was the getting-to-know-one-another phase of their relationship, the consummation, as it were, came out of shared vulnerability. The two ended up in a writing group, sharing material back and forth. That’s when they finally read one another’s work, and their perspective shifted. Kelly, who had come to USC from small town roots in both Hawaii and Washington state without much of a plan before the screenwriting program took him in, was similarly moved by Lanzing’s work. “I'm realizing the story he wrote was my experience, he says. “This is a brother, not a foe. Embrace him like a brother. From that moment on, that respect changed the dynamic of our relationship.”

The pair spent more and more time together, especially after they graduated and took a road trip to Lollapalooza to see Radiohead—which Kelly wryly describes as “pots and pans being tossed down the stairs music”—where their respect for one another grew. “I have so much respect for who he is as a creator, " Kelly says. “It's almost like they say, Don't meet your heroes, but it's like, I kind of just get to hang out with one of my heroes all the time.” Lanzing quickly chimes in, saying, “ I just had never met somebody who thought the way Collin did . . . I learned pretty early, not as a writing partner, but as a friend, he filled in a lot of my gaps.”

In those early days, the pair didn’t always have the language to express the depths of their friendship to one another, with both agreeing it was easier to pour that into the work and have it manifest there.

“We were able to have that rich emotional relationship without saying those words exactly because we were able to funnel it all through our characters,” Kelly adds. “We were almost forced by the fact that we had pledged our careers to each other. We were like, the only way we're going to get through this life is together, making beautiful stories together, making things that are tragic and real and sincere. That necessitates us opening up and being real and tragic and sincere with each other in a way that's like, whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, this is just for the story, man.”

THE AFOREMENTIONED LOLLAPALOOZA trip turned out to be beneficial not only in furthering the pair’s friendship, but giving them a real foot in the door in Hollywood. As they drove from Los Angeles to Chicago, the boys started riffing on story ideas, eventually hitting on their shared love of Akira Kurosawa movies and Japanese culture. On the road, they put together an outline for a movie called Sundown about seven samurai defending a town from Daki, aka Japanese vampires. “Ultimately, it's about this guy having to kill his best friend,” Lanzing says. “We didn’t really realize we were writing a lot of the early parts of our relationship into the script.”

By the time the trip back to LA concluded, the duo thought Sundown was in good-but-not-great shape. Kelly had a deal with William Morris, and brought the script to his agent there with the understanding that any sale involving the story was now a package deal. While the movie ultimately never got made, it made enough of an impression to get them recurring work, even as the industry shifted in real time, often being tapped to work on web series, which became all the rage after the 2008 financial crisis.

The two worked part-time on storytelling while holding full-time jobs. That schedule meant they’d get together for face-to-face working sessions on Thursday and all day Sunday. “Our wives, our friends, everybody had to accept the fact that, look, if you want Jack or Collin on [those days], you don't get them,” Kelly says.

With such a complicated working arrangement, the possibility of not working as a duo did come up. At one point, Kelly took a chance to co-write an animation with another writer friend, but the production ended up spanning six different time zones. Fundamentally, the project was messing and began taking a toll on Kelly, to the point where it finally came to a head.

“It genuinely is one of the only times I’ve gotten angry at Collin,” Lanzing adds. “That’s the one time I’ve ever had to deploy it in our relationship because it had literally gotten to the point where it was like, he’s disappearing. Not just into this project but into himself.”

Lanzing found it to be the “scariest” moment in their entire relationship. “I think that is legit one of the first times we were ever really emotionally vulnerable with another,” he says. “The crazy thing is, I think it actually brought us closer together.”

“Oh, yeah,” Kelly interjects. “I was scream crying.”

“We lost it at each other and were able to put it back together,” Lanzing says, picking the thread back up. “I think it taught us both, like, okay, we can do this.”

A FEW YEARS ago, DC Comics published a series of Batman-related one-shots. The series, titled “One Bad Day,” draws inspiration from Alan Moore, Brian Bolland, and John Higgins’ seminal The Killing Joke story. In the story, the Joker rolls out his MO, a fitting bit of text that’s become totemic within comic book lore: “All it takes is one bad day to reduce the sanest man alive to lunacy. That’s how far the world is from where I am. Just one bad day.”

The one-shots featured a handful of stories, all told from the point of view of a Batman villain. Kelly and Lanzing’s story, drawn by Xermanico, follows the Basil Karlo version of Clayface, who is on the verge of a breakout role and slowly descends into madness as he kills more and more people in the film industry to get what he wants. It’s also clearly one of the main sources of inspiration for the DCU’s new body horror film Clayface, which released earlier this month to the excitement of DC fans (and landing at the top of the box office). The film follows a version of Clayface named Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) and his quest for continued fame on the silver screen (even with plenty of body mutations and murders coming along the way).

Kelly says that DC reached out to them specifically because of their Hollywood background—and thought that would be perfect for Clayface. “Talk about taking our trauma and doing our therapy—that book is taking all the pain that we've had and expressing it through the character and taking him through something really genuinely emotional and horrifying,” Kelly says. “And it has nothing to do with being a Clayface.”

But for both men, the book is another kind of cautionary tale. It’s what could have happened to them if they hadn’t found one another. “[Basil] kills and impersonates his supposed best friend,” Lanzing says. “That's the pivot point. That's the thing that makes it not Collin and I's story. Rather than look at the other guy and be like, I want the jobs you have, I want the opportunities you have, I want the talent you have, I want the ideas you have, I want the life you have, I want the face you have. Rather than doing any of that, what we did was we said, What if we take the monetary sacrifice involved in splitting that fifty-fifty, but then do it together and make an alliance that doesn't break, that doesn't lead to one of us stuffing the other one in the back of a car? Does that lead to a better outcome? “At this point, we’re getting to the part of the summit that seems like it led to a better outcome.”

Based on the expansive depth and breadth of their work, the answer is a resounding yes. But in how the two men talk about one another, and their friendship, and what they’ve meant to one another, even without creating together, it’s the kind of relationship anyone would love to have. A perfect partnership where each brings out the best in the other, resulting in something that transcends and goes beyond—even if maintaining and cultivating that relationship can sometimes get tricky or rocky, it’s worth it. Being in a foxhole with someone else is always going to be better than doing it alone.

#4837. Kia’s electric SUV and van are getting a new job as police cars

Kia’s electric vehicles could soon be the ones pulling you over. Kia converted the EV5 and PV5 into patrol vehicles as part of its push for greener police cars.

Electric vehicles make great police cars — they have instant torque, require less maintenance, and are nearly silent.

Several police departments have used electric patrol cars for years, including the Ford Mustang Mach-E and Tesla Model Y.

Kia is eyeing the market with its midsize electric SUV and van. At the 2026 International Public Security Industry Exhibition in South Korea, Kia showcased two patrol vehicle concepts based on the EV5 and PV5.

The EV5 and PV5 patrol car concepts feature custom lights, sirens, and dedicated police badging on the side.

This year’s theme was “A New Era of K-Public Security by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotics,” so Kia took the opportunity to showcase its latest security equipment and tech.

Kia said the EV5 is a perfect fit for police use, offering “best-in-class” interior space and luggage capacity of up to 965 liters. It features an added luggage board to store equipment and other supplies.

Earlier this year, Kia developed AI patrol cars with the Korean National Police Agency and has been holding training programs to implement electric vehicles.

The AI Patrol Car is based on the PV5, Kia’s 5-seat electric van. The PV5 AI Patrol Vehicle is equipped with three 4K AI cameras and even a drone landing pad mounted on the roof.

The cameras located on the front and rear of the vehicle use AI to detect dangerous situations and automatically alert the driver.

For example, the system can identify guns, knives, bats, and other weapons, as well as emergencies in which someone collapses.

The electric patrol van is equipped with a roof-mounted drone for ground surveillance, while the docking station charges it on the go. The drones have advanced thermal imaging cameras with 90X zoom that can read license plates and pinpoint someone on the run.

Kia’s AI Patrol Cars have been in operation by the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency’s Wide Area Prevention Patrol Division since last July.

“We intend to showcase the competitiveness of Kia’s electrified mobility and its potential for use as police patrol vehicles,” a Kia official said. The company plans to continue developing custom solutions for police and other public sector use based on its electric vehicles.

#4836. Latest Analysis: Circumcision Boosts Men’s Sexual Function

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Circumcision is controversial, sexually and psychologically.

It involves surgical removal of the foreskin, the skin that covers the head (glans) of the penis. The foreskin contains touch-sensitive nerves. By removing them, circumcision opponents insist that it must reduce the penis’ sexual sensitivity and impair men’s pleasure. On Reddit and other Internet forums, opponents have denounced circumcision as barbarous, unfair to male infants, and physically and psychologically harmful.

Supporters counter that the vast majority of erotically sensitive nerve endings are located in the glans, not the foreskin, and that the procedure does not compromise men’s sexual function or pleasure. Recently, Turkish researchers analyzed 15 studies of circumcision and found that far from impairing men sexually, it enhances men’s sexual function.

The investigators conducted a meta-analysis of 15 previously published studies. Meta-analysis is a standard statistical technique that allows the results of small studies to be combined as if they’d all been one large trial. Study size is important. The larger the study population, the more likely the results are to reflect reality. The 15 studies involved 14,737 men, a number that lends credibility to the findings. The meta-analysis showed that, compared with men with intact foreskins, those who were circumcised reported greater sexual satisfaction (p < 0.001), improved erection function (p = 0.002), less pain during intercourse (p = 0.03), and fewer orgasm difficulties (p = 0.01) (Karaahmet and Lalaeh, 2025).

The researchers evaluated 15 studies, but many more have been conducted. How did they select those 15? They used the World Health Organization’s (WHO) guidelines for grading research rigor and chose only the most credible studies, which is important as many studies of circumcision’s sexual impact have been biased either for or against the procedure.

These reports don’t inspire much confidence.

Circumcision reduces the risk of AIDS (below). Several studies have involved before-and-after surveys of African men circumcised as adults to reduce AIDS risk:

But these studies are also problematic. When they were conducted, AIDS was epidemic in Africa, and many participants feared for their lives. Researchers reassured them that circumcision had no sexual downsides. Critics charged that circumcised subjects felt so relieved to have their AIDS risk reduced that they parroted back what the researchers had told them—that circumcision has no sexual impact.

Using WHO guidelines, the authors of the new report excluded many studies, both pro and con, such as those just mentioned, and included only the most methodologically rigorous studies, which showed that circumcision causes no discernible sexual impairment.

Worldwide, one-third of men are circumcised. Judaism and Islam require it, so in Israel and across the Muslim world, the practice is virtually universal. Circumcision is also popular in the U.S. and Asia, but less so in Europe, Latin America, and non-Muslim Africa.

Jews and Muslims have circumcised boys for centuries. During the 19th century, the practice spread to Christians who believed—mistakenly—that it prevented masturbation. Circumcision is not medically necessary, but it offers health benefits in several areas:

These findings have prompted some Jews and Muslims to claim their faiths were medically prescient and required circumcision for health reasons. But theologians of both religions insist that the practice has always been an act of faith and so its medical benefits, while welcome, are coincidental.

For the vast majority of men, the controversy over circumcision and sexual function is moot. They’re either circumcised or not, and if so, the vast majority have lived that way since infancy and have no way to compare their sexual sensitivity before and after the procedure.

If you’re intact and want to believe you have superior erotic sensitivity, you’re free to feel smug. But the weight of the evidence shows that circumcision does not impair sexual function, and that circumcised men have no reason to fear they’re missing out on erotic pleasure and satisfaction.

Karaahmet, AY and SS Lalaeh. “The Influence of Circumcision on Male Sexual Function: A Meta-Analysis of Satisfaction, Erectile Function, and Dyspareunia,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2025) 51:551. Doi: 10.1080/0092623X.2025.2499141

Armagan, A. et al. “Circumcision During the Phallic Period: Does It Affect the Psychosexual Functions in Adulthood?" Andrologia (2014) 46:254.

Bollinger, D., and R.S. Van Howe. “Alexithymia and Circumcision Trauma: A Preliminary Investigation,” International Journal of Men’s Health (2011) 10:184.

Bossio, J.A. et al. “Examining Penile Sensitivity in Neonatally Circumcised and Intact Men Using Quantitative Sensory Testing,” Journal of Urology (2016) 195:1848.

Bronselaer, G.A. et al. “Male Circumcision Decreases Penile Sensitivity As Measured in a Large Cohort,” BJU International (2013) 111:820.

Cortes-Gonzalez, J.R. et al. “Does Circumcision Affect Male’s Perception of Sexual Satisfaction?” Arch. Esp. Urol. (2009) 62:733.

Dias, J. et al. “Adult Circumcision and Male Sexual Health: A Retrospective Analysis,” Andrologia (2014) 46:459.

Homfray, V. et al. “Examining the Association Between Male Circumcision and Sexual Function: Evidence from a British Probability Survey,” AIDS (2015) 29:1411.

Hoschke, B. et al. “Male Circumcision Is Not Associated with an Increased Prevalence of Erectile Dysfunction: Results of the Cottbus 10,000 Men Survey,” Der Urologe (2013) 52:562.

Kigozi, G. et al. “The Effect of Male Circumcision on Sexual Satisfaction and Function: Results from a Randomized Trial of Male Circumcision for Human Immunodeficiency Virus Prevention in Rakai, Uganda,” BJU [formerly British Journal of Urology] (2008) 101:65. Doi:10.1111/j.1464-410X.2007.07369.x

Krieger, J.N. et al. “Adult Male Circumcision: Effects on Sexual Function and Satisfaction in Kisumu, Kenya,” Journal of Sexual Medicine (2008) 5:2610.

Morris, B.J. et al. “Does Male Circumcision Affect Sexual Function, Sensitivity, or Satisfaction? A Systematic Review,” Journal of Sexual Medicine (2013) 10:2644.

Shabanzadeh, D.M. et al. “Male Circumcision Does Not Result in Inferior Perceived Male Sexual Function: A Systematic Review,” Danish Medical Journal (2016) 63:pii:A5245.

Tian, Y. et al. “Effects of Circumcision on Male Sexual Functions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis,” Asian Journal of Andrology (2013) 15:662.

#4834. Simone Biles Thought Her Itchy, Flaky Scalp Was Dandruff. It Was Eczema

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles is the most decorated gymnast in history. But the beloved icon is taking a break from talking about the balance beam and vault to discuss a personal health condition that she lives with alongside 31 million fellow Americans: eczema.

“A couple years ago, I started noticing flaking and itching on my scalp, especially on the crown of my head. And at first, I thought it was a lot of dandruff, and then I was worried it could be something contagious,” Biles told Healthline. “I’ve also dealt with patches of dry skin on my arm, but it comes and goes.”

Recently, she noticed her symptoms getting worse, especially when stressed from training.

“I would definitely be in the gym, finding myself waiting for bars or for beam and just scratching and scratching and [people] would be like, ‘Simone, can you stop scratching?’ and I’m like, ‘Oh, yeah, my bad, sorry,’” said Biles.

When her hairdresser noticed scaly patches on her scalp, Biles began searching online for answers and trying home remedies, including combs, shampoos, and oils.

“[Self-fixes] weren’t really helping, and I didn’t go to the dermatologist immediately because I was busy in the gym training,” said Biles. “I also felt ashamed and embarrassed, so I started speaking out about it at Paris Olympics.”

After making a TikTok video about her symptoms, she was inspired to see a dermatologist who diagnosed her with the skin conditions seborrheic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis (also known as eczema).

“[A] lot of what she is communicating really mirrors what we’re seeing in patients and what we know about these conditions,” Angela Lamb, MD, Bile’s dermatologist, told Healthline.

While eczema is a group of chronic inflammatory skin conditions, Lamb said stress can trigger flares, as well as extremes of weather, especially for those with atopic dermatitis.

“And then there’s just individual triggers, so patients really need to listen to their bodies, find out what moisturizer would work well for their skin, find out if you have seborrheic dermatitis on your scalp,” said Lamb. “[Know] what are the products that tend to be flaring it or what you do that makes it better or worse.”

Biles says she found relief for her symptoms with Zoryve, a once-daily, steroid-free, topical prescription medication that comes in both foam and cream forms. Biles uses both forms: the foam for her scalp, and the cream for her skin.

“I feel like it fits in easily to my lifestyle…you can apply it to your scalp, and it’s really, really lightweight, and then for my eczema, it’s a cream, and it’s non-greasy,” said Biles.

In addition to helping her feel more comfortable, she said that receiving effective treatment eased the embarrassment she experienced around the appearance of her skin.

“[Going] on a lot of shoots and a lot of sets, [I was] definitely more self-conscious about my parts or if I was wearing braids — the flaking, what that looks like on camera — so I would just try to cover it up with oils and all of that stuff,” she said.

To share her journey, Biles partnered with Zoryve’s maker, Arcutis Biotherapeutics, to launch its Skin to Believe In campaign. The initiative aims to break the stigma around chronic skin conditions that can make people feel self-conscious, isolated, or embarrassed.

“I know people are going through similar things, thinking it’s dandruff or thinking it’s contagious,” Biles said. “[You] don’t have to silently suffer. Own it. Go see a trusted professional, and get the relief that you deserve.”

Because every medication has potential side effects, Lamb said it’s important to talk with your doctor about a medication’s potential risks and benefits.

“This one, the side effects are in a very low percent of patients, which can include some nausea, headache, as well as an allergic reaction, but you’ll discuss that with your physician, and in this case, dermatologists are the main ones writing for Zoryve,” said Lamb.

She said it’s encouraging that nonsteroidal medications exist as options for patients with skin conditions. She explained that Zoryve contains roflumilast, a PDE4 inhibitor that helps reduce inflammation involved in eczema.

“So I’m very excited [because] I think the landscape of how we’re treating many conditions is really changing as we understand the science and the core of what drives it better,” said Lamb. “I think that’s been the largest breakthrough in the last many years in healthcare…understanding root cause is better, which can lead us to better treatments.”

Because Biles believes stress can contribute to her eczema flares, she practices a wellness routine that includes spending time with her girlfriends to get their nails done or a massage, and taking baths at night to wind down.

“[But] honestly, without training every single day, I don’t feel as stressed,” she said. “[Everyone] can find different ways to alleviate their stress. And it looks different for everyone.”

As she approaches her 30th birthday, Biles says she’s learned to prioritize her physical and mental well-being.

“I feel like now I know that there is help out there if I do get stuck or I notice something, and I feel like maturity has helped a lot with that,” she said.

“And I just feel like being an ambassador and having awareness for so much has opened up the doors for me to say, ‘Hey, I’m not feeling okay. Can I please do this instead?’ Or, ‘Oh, I need to speak to my therapist twice a week because I feel like I’m stuck in a rut right now.’ So I feel like [aging] has given me space and… confidence to do that.”

#4833. Finding the Tailwinds That Help Us Move Forward

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

So often, our attention gravitates toward what is wrong, challenging, or missing. Yet when we focus solely on what is not working, we lose sight of the things that are helping us along.

I find it helpful to think about the headwinds and tailwinds moving through our lives.

Headwinds are the pressures, stressors, and challenges that push against us. They are the things coming at us, demanding our attention, threatening to knock us off course, or making it harder to move in the direction we want to go. Some are temporary, while others are part of circumstances we cannot quickly change. Tailwinds are the forces supporting us from behind and within. They include our strengths, skills, relationships, routines, experiences, and values that help us keep going. They may not remove the headwinds, but they can help us meet them with greater support and perspective.

In Stress Wisely, I explore wellness through eight interconnected dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, environmental, occupational, financial, and spiritual. Each offers a different lens through which we're able to notice what is hindering us, what is helping us, and where we might find room for growth.

Wellness is an ongoing process of understanding what we need, noticing what supports us, and making adjustments as our circumstances change. Perhaps we are not sleeping as well as we would like, feel disconnected from the people we care about, are carrying financial stress, or have lost touch with the activities that give our lives meaning. These concerns deserve our attention, and sometimes they call for change, additional support, or a closer look at what is possible within our circumstances. At the same time, my gentle invitation is to ask ourselves: What is already working for me here?

It is easy to focus on what our bodies are not able to do or what we wish we could change, but we can also appreciate what they help us experience and what we are doing to care for them. Perhaps a 30-minute walk every day helps you clear your mind, a consistent bedtime is allowing you to show up with better energy, or you've learned to recognize when you are running on empty and need to slow down. These everyday choices matter.

If you thought of your body as a vehicle carrying you through life, what is helping you take good care of it and keep it going?

Emotional wellness is about learning to recognize our feelings and respond to them with greater understanding instead of ignoring them or expecting ourselves to push through them. One tailwind may be your growing ability to name what you are feeling. Maybe you give yourself 90 seconds to sit with an emotion and let it move through you, find comfort in a creative outlet, or reach out to a trusted person rather than carrying everything alone. These are ways of making room for our emotions as we navigate the hard parts.

What helps you process your feelings and meet yourself with a little more compassion?

We learn through curiosity, reflection, conversation, and experience. Each and every one of us has skills we've developed over time, mistakes we've learned from, and different perspectives we've opened ourselves up to that have broadened our thinking.

Thinking of a particular area in your life, what have you learned, figured out, or become more capable of doing?

We are not meant to navigate life alone. A friend who checks in, a colleague who understands, or a community where we feel we belong can remind us we are supported and valued. We can also notice the strengths we bring to our relationships, such as being a good listener, a thoughtful encourager, or a practical problem-solver. Connection is about the support we receive, but it's also about the ways we contribute to one another.

Who helps you feel safe, seen, and supported? What do you bring to the relationships that matter to you?

Our surroundings can influence how we feel and move through our days. We can't always change our environment, but we can notice the places that bring a little ease. Maybe it's a favourite park bench, a sunny spot by your living room window, or a calm corner where you can collect your thoughts. Creating and spending time in hope-filled havens that offer comfort and inspiration can make a difference.

Which places help you feel more settled, connected, or at ease?

Our contributions extend beyond paid work to include caregiving, parenting, volunteering, and the many responsibilities that make up our days. When the demands feel relentless, we may overlook the care we bring to our work, the problems we have solved, or the difference we make in the lives of others. A tailwind might be recognizing a task you carry out that makes someone else's day easier, setting a boundary around email, asking for support, keeping a commitment that reflects your values, or celebrating the small wins.

Where do you find meaning in the work you get to do, and what helps you do it in a sustainable way?

When financial pressures are weighing on us, it can be hard to see what we're doing well and what is working for us. Recognizing what's helping us doesn't mean pretending those worries aren't real. Perhaps you have become more aware of your spending, started a conversation you've been avoiding, learned something about budgeting, or reached out to understand your options.

What is helping you feel more informed, supported, or prepared when it comes to your resources?

Spiritual wellness can be rooted in faith, and it can also be found in our values, sense of purpose, and connection to something larger than ourselves. Noticing the moments that remind us of what matters most can help us make choices that reflect it. Maybe it's spending time in nature, being of service, a prayer practice or familiar ritual, or making time for the people and causes you care about.

When do you feel most connected to what matters most to you?

We cannot always choose what life brings our way. Yet even when things feel difficult, we can widen our view so that what is hard is not the only thing we see.

This is where I believe gratitude is one of the mightiest forces we have for living well. It draws our attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, helping us recognize what is sustaining us today and what we can carry forward into tomorrow.

Hanley-Dafoe, R. (2023). Stress wisely: How to be well in an unwell world. Page Two.

#4832. BMW’s first three-row electric SUV is almost here: Here’s an early look at the iX7

BMW is preparing to introduce its first three-row electric SUV. With its official debut coming up, the iX7 was spotted testing, offering a sneak peek at the full-size luxury SUV.

The iX7 is the electric version of BMW’s largest and most luxurious SUV. Although BMW has yet to announce it officially, disguised prototypes were recently caught testing at the Nürburgring in Germany.

After the iX3 and iX5, the iX7 is the next BMW SUV in line to debut with its Neue Klasse technology and design.

Like the iX5, BMW’s three-row electric SUV will retain a more traditional style than the full-on Neue Klasse EVs, such as the iX3.

BMW will reveal details closer to its debut, expected in mid-2027. Like the smaller iX5 60 xDrive, the iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. #4831. A Former College Athlete’s Battle With Depression

He spent years trying to power through his depression, cycling through several traditional oral antidepressants, before finding a medication that worked for him.

JEREMIAH FELT GLUED to his couch, too sad and unmotivated to move. He was supposed to be getting ready for his wedding—a day when he expected to feel more confident than ever. Instead, his groomsmen had to come to his apartment and help him get there. A former college athlete, Jeremiah was still a big guy, and it took all of them to lift him from the couch and carry him out the door.

It’s not what you think. Jeremiah had absolutely no doubts about marrying the love of his life. He was in the throes of a depressive episode, one of many he had experienced dating back several years. For Jeremiah, becoming a husband meant becoming a provider and protector. But on the day he was supposed to step into that role, he was the one who needed help—and he felt ashamed.

The wedding-day episode was just one part of a much longer struggle. Jeremiah’s symptoms first appeared in college and worsened after graduation. When he entered the workforce, his symptoms worsened and he became exhausted and increasingly apathetic—to the point of neglecting his hygiene. Eventually, he became too depressed to get out of bed in the morning and lost his first job.

In 2012, Jeremiah was officially diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD), a mental health condition that can have a significant impact on daily life and make it difficult to find motivation or energy for self-care. Over the next nine years, persistent symptoms made it difficult for him to maintain employment, and he eventually went on disability.

DEPRESSION IN MEN often hides in plain sight. In 2021, 6.2 percent of U.S. adult men and 10.3 percent of U.S. adult women experienced a major depressive episode, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

Those numbers tell us how common depression is, but not what it looks like. Men and women can experience many of the same symptoms, including sadness, hopelessness, fatigue, changes in sleep, and loss of interest in favorite activities. However, depression often shows up differently in men. Feeling sad or emotional isn’t always the main symptom. For many men, symptoms can show up as headaches, digestive problems, tiredness, irritability, or long-term pain. Feeling isolated or seeking distractions to avoid dealing with feelings or relationships can also be signs.

According to Craig Chepke, MD, DFAPA, a psychiatrist and medical director based in Huntersville, North Carolina, men may have a hard time talking about their feelings and asking for help, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. “Depression in men is often missed or misread, including by men and others close to them, because it doesn’t always look like what people expect depression to look like,” he explains. “Instead of sadness, it may show up as irritability, anger, withdrawal, or self-medication. Sometimes it takes an ultimatum from someone who cares about them just to get them into the office. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw, but I hear men with depression say variations of the same thing over and over: ‘If I was just stronger, I’d be able to handle this on my own.’”

Jeremiah agrees. “You feel like less of a man, like you should be able to just power through somehow, or snap out of it,” he says. “But you can’t. You don’t. Depression affects your confidence in every aspect of your life. It becomes a dehumanizing experience.”

BEYOND HIS OWN self-doubt, Jeremiah had a hard time finding healthcare providers who would take his symptoms seriously. He dealt with therapists who minimized his struggles. One provider even attributed his symptoms to restless legs syndrome.

At times, Jeremiah felt that some doctors viewed depression as a “woman’s disease,” subtly calling his masculinity into question. Being a Black man added another layer as he navigated a healthcare system that didn’t always understand his experience.

He experienced more difficulty when he opened up to loved ones. “Being a man is lonely in general. There are very few men you can talk to beneath the surface level about things even though you call each other friends. I shared my struggle with MDD with my two closest friends, and it kind of freaked them out,” he says. “We didn’t talk much after that for about a year.” He received a similar reaction from cousins and extended family members, who weren’t sure what to say or whether to treat him differently. Things improved once they saw that his personality hadn’t fundamentally changed.

Jeremiah’s marriage, however, became a turning point. His wife, a clinical therapist, was uniquely positioned to recognize his condition. Starting around 2016, she began noticing subtle changes, how he would pick up and lose interest in activities and hobbies, and how Jeremiah would withdraw into himself around the house. It was then that she encouraged him to seek professional help. But asking for help was only the beginning. Finding a treatment that adequately addressed his symptoms would take years.

IN 2021, JEREMIAH was diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which affects about 30 percent of people with MDD. TRD is generally defined as MDD that has not resolved after trying at least two traditional oral antidepressants. “By the time someone checks off medication after medication on an intake form, they’ve usually lost something more valuable than time,” Dr. Chepke says of people living with TRD. “They’ve lost hope that anything can get better.”

Jeremiah knew his feelings were real. “TRD is a bully and it will hit you in the face from the moment you wake up,” he says. “Your best days are not behind you. You’re just going through something that a lot of men go through and just aren't able to admit it. You’re working to hold onto the life you want to live, not just your health, but your lifestyle, who you want to be, and the type of man you want to become or already are.”

For a while, Jeremiah kept trying new medications and started losing hope when they didn’t work. But with help from his wife and doctor, he found a different path.

LOOKING BACK, WHAT mattered most to Jeremiah was his wife’s consistent support through the process. In the early years of treatment, she helped him remember appointments and his medication schedules that kept him moving forward when motivation was scarce. Jeremiah’s doctor recommended he try SPRAVATO® (esketamine), an FDA-approved nasal spray for adults with TRD, used alone or with an oral antidepressant.

It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective for use in preventing suicide or in reducing suicidal thoughts or actions. SPRAVATO® is not for use in place of hospitalization if your healthcare provider determines that hospitalization is needed, even if improvement is experienced after the first dose of SPRAVATO®. SPRAVATO® is not for use as a medicine to prevent or relieve pain (anesthetic). It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe or effective as an anesthetic medicine. It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective in children. (Please see additional Important Safety Information including Boxed WARNINGS, limitations of use, and a list of side effects below. Click here to learn more.)

SPRAVATO is only available through a restricted distribution program called the SPRAVATO Risk Evaluation & Mitigation Strategy (REMS). SPRAVATO can only be administered at a certified healthcare setting, and patients self-administer the pre-filled nasal device at a REMS-certified treatment center under direct clinical supervision and are monitored for at least two hours after taking SPRAVATO. SPRAVATO may have serious side effects such as sedation, dissociation, and respiratory depression, and the risk of abuse and misuse.

SPRAVATO represents a different treatment approach for TRD. Unlike traditional antidepressants that work on serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, SPRAVATO acts on glutamate, a chemical messenger in the brain that is thought to regulate depression. The role of glutamate in depression and the exact way SPRAVATO works are unknown.

As his depressive symptoms improved, Jeremiah began to engage more with others. He also joined a support group for Black men navigating these challenges. Hearing other people’s stories reminds him that he’s not alone. Today, he works as an IT and cybersecurity instructor in Chicago, speaks at industry conferences, and builds robots in his spare time.

Jeremiah’s experience is his own, and treatment decisions are personal. “There’s no one treatment that’s right for everybody,” Dr. Chepke says. In his practice, Dr. Chepke has witnessed reductions in certain patients’ depressive symptoms when incorporating SPRAVATO into their treatment. While not all of his patients may benefit, seeing some move from repeatedly cycling through different treatments to an option studied specifically for TRD has helped shape how he approaches care for this population.

If you haven’t found relief from your depressive symptoms, talk with your doctor about the options that may be appropriate for you—and most importantly, know that there is hope.

#4830. Tesla (TSLA) releases Q3 2026 financial results: margins rebound, profit still falls

Tesla (TSLA) released its financial results and shareholders’ letter for the third quarter (Q3) 2026 after market close today. We’re updating this post with all the details from the financial results, shareholders’ letter, and the conference call later tonight.

The earnings call with management is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. ET.

Wall Street came into the report expecting a flat quarter. The FactSet consensus, as displayed on Estimize, called for $28.06 billion in revenue, essentially unchanged from the $28.1 billion Tesla posted in Q3 2025 and a bit below the $28.24 billion it reported last quarter.

Profit expectations were lower. Analysts were looking for non-GAAP earnings of $0.45 per share, down 10% from $0.50 a year ago. The Estimize crowd was slightly more bullish at $28.36 billion and $0.48.

We already had the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2.1% year-over-year but well ahead of the 461,974 consensus, while producing only 464,391. It also deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago but short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected. For the full setup, see our Q3 2026 earnings preview.

So the question was never volume. It was whether Tesla could stop the profit slide after Q2, when operating margin fell to 1.4% and EPS missed the consensus by 20 cents.

After the market closed today, Tesla released its financial results for the third quarter and reported $28.05 billion in revenue, flat from a year ago and in line with the $28.06 billion Wall Street expected. Non-GAAP earnings came in at $0.48 per share, beating the $0.45 consensus but down 4% from $0.50 a year ago.

It’s a better quarter than Q2, but the trend hasn’t changed. Margins recovered, with auto gross margin excluding credits back above 18%, yet operating income still fell 56% year-over-year as spending on AI and Optimus grew faster than gross profit. On a GAAP basis, net income dropped 43% to $787 million, or $0.22 per share.

Total gross margin was 19.6%, up 160 basis points from 18.0% a year ago and well above the 16.8% Tesla posted in Q2. Operating income fell 56% to $718 million, for an operating margin of 2.6%, compared with 5.8% a year ago and 1.4% last quarter.

Operating expenses came in at $4.78 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Research and development alone jumped 69% to $2.76 billion as Tesla spends on what it now calls “Super Intelligence” (SI), Optimus, and the Cybercab. Stock-based compensation, which includes the 2025 CEO pay package, hit $1.17 billion, up from $663 million a year ago.

Capital spending was $4.73 billion, more than double the $2.25 billion of a year ago, and free cash flow came in at $1.53 billion, compared with $3.99 billion a year ago and negative $1.09 billion in Q2. Tesla ended the quarter with $45.4 billion in cash and investments. GAAP net income included a $288 million unrealized gain on Tesla’s bitcoin holdings, partly offset by a $142 million unrealized loss on its SpaceX equity investment.

That puts Tesla’s capex at $13.01 billion through the first nine months of 2026, only about half of the “more than $25 billion” management guided for the year. To hit that number, Tesla would need to spend roughly $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter so far. The Q3 letter doesn’t update the guidance, and capex actually fell sequentially from $5.79 billion in Q2. So either Q4 spending explodes, or the 2026 plan is quietly slipping into 2027. The lower spending also flatters this quarter’s positive free cash flow.

The number we watch first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits, now that the credit market has mostly dried up. It came in at 18.1% this quarter, up from 16.3% in Q2 and 15.4% a year ago, though still below the 19.2% of Q1, when Tesla got help from warranty and tariff one-time benefits. Tesla credits a better regional and product mix and more FSD subscription revenue, partly offset by lower average selling prices.

Regulatory credits brought in just $113 million, down 73% from $417 million a year ago and below the $146 million in Q2. That line isn’t coming back now that automakers no longer pay federal fuel-economy penalties.

Energy was the weak spot on revenue. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion, which Tesla partly blames on tariff-related customer refunds, even though deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh. The segment’s gross margin jumped to 33% from 20% in Q2, but energy gross profit still slipped to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago.

Services and other was the bright spot. Revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion, and Tesla says gross profit hit a record $734 million on charging, insurance and parts sales.

Tesla says “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter,” and that it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.”

That’s a new explanation for flat sales. Deliveries were still down 2% year-over-year, “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi, Model S and X) fell 48%, and Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it built, bringing inventory down to 11 days of supply from 15 in Q2. But average selling prices fell again, which isn’t usually what a supply-constrained automaker does.

On autonomy, Tesla says active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, as defined in Musk’s 2025 pay package. Its Robotaxi service reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the quarter, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet.

I am still waiting for the 50% YOY growth rate that Musk touted a few years ago to justify the TSLA valuation. Then I reminded myself that TSLA is just the largest MEME stock in the market day.

Tesla’s full Q3 2026 shareholder deck is available on the company’s investor relations site, and management will discuss the results on the earnings call at 5:30 p.m. ET.

This is a developing story. We’ll add the most important updates from Tesla’s shareholder letter and earnings call here as they come.

#4828. Tesla blames battery supply for flat sales, but its prices keep falling

Tesla says battery supply, not demand, is what’s holding back its car sales. In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, the automaker wrote that “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter.”

It also claims it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.” But the numbers in the same letter don’t line up with a company that has more buyers than cars.

The battery line has been building for a while. In Q2, Tesla called battery pack capacity “the main limiting factor to near-term vehicle production volume increase.” Now it says batteries limited what it could sell during the quarter itself.

Tesla didn’t put a number on the backlog. It did list record deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan, and record production at Gigafactory Berlin. Elsewhere in the Q3 2026 financial results, Tesla says it is focused on “increasing production across our factories” because of “strong demand.”

Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, down 2% from 497,099 a year ago. Model 3 and Model Y were down 1%. “Other models,” which covers Cybertruck, Semi and what’s left of Model S and X, fell 48% to 8,295 units.

It built 464,391 vehicles, so it delivered 22,141 more than it produced. That’s the second quarter in a row Tesla has worked down inventory, after building about 50,000 more cars than it sold in Q1. Global inventory fell to 11 days of supply, from 27 days in Q1 and 15 in Q2.

Model 3 and Model Y production ran at about 1.83 million units annualized. Tesla lists more than 2.25 million units of installed capacity for those two models across Fremont, Shanghai, Berlin and Texas. So the factories ran at roughly 81%.

And here’s the part that doesn’t fit. In its list of reasons revenue didn’t grow, Tesla cited “lower vehicle average selling price (ASP)” year-over-year, even after excluding currency effects. Automakers that can’t build cars fast enough usually raise prices, or at least stop discounting.

Tesla has more places to put battery cells than it used to. The same letter says energy storage had its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and Tesla is increasing 4680 cell output “to support the ramps of both Cybercab and Tesla Semi along with higher Model Y volumes.”

Tesla’s outlook even says deliveries depend on “allocation decisions between sale to customers and use for our owned and operated fleet.” So part of the battery constraint is Tesla deciding where its cells go.

Battery supply is a real issue, and tariffs on Chinese cells make it harder in the US. Tesla also did set records in a few markets, but overall deliveries are down, and Tesla is selling cars for lower than it used to. Those are not signs of a company that is supply constrained.

That is the excuses to spin. It doesn't matter what Musk says, his supporters will believe it.

In fact, today, in 2026, Tesla has more battery suppliers than ever, and it has itself ramped up production of its own battery cells.

But “we’re supply constrained” is one of Tesla’s oldest lines, and this letter doesn’t prove it. Deliveries fell year-over-year. Prices fell. Two quarters ago, Tesla built 50,000 cars it couldn’t sell. If batteries were really the bottleneck, Tesla would be raising prices and keeping the extra margin, not lowering ASPs.

The more likely answer is that it’s a bit of both. Demand recovered somewhat in some markets, and Tesla is choosing to send more cells to Megapack, Cybercab and Semi because it thinks those businesses are worth more. That’s a reasonable strategy. #4827. 8-Hour Time-Restricted Eating Window May Lead to Greater Weight Loss

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Limiting your eating to an 8-hour window may result in more weight loss than a 12-hour window, according to a new study published in the journal Nutrition & Diabetes on September 12.

Time-restricted eating (TRE) is a form of intermittent fasting that limits eating to a set daily window, such as 8, 10, or 12 hours, without necessarily changing what you eat.

The eating window is followed by fasting for the remaining hours. Common approaches include 16:8, which involves 16 hours of fasting and 8 hours of eating, and early TRE, which involves eating earlier in the day.

The researchers used data from 124 adults across five TRE trials lasting between 3 and 6 months. At baseline, participants had an average eating window of about 15 hours and at least one component of metabolic syndrome.

Their food and beverage intake was tracked using an app.

Participants were assigned either to a TRE group or to the control group. The control group participants maintained their habitual intake, received nutritional counseling, or were given guidance on healthy eating.

Those in the TRE group limited their eating windows to 8, 10, or 12 hours, with no restrictions on dietary quality or energy intake.

After 3–6 months, the researchers found that participants assigned to an 8-hour eating window lost about 3.7 pounds (1.7 kg) more than those assigned to a 12-hour window and about 5 pounds (2.3 kg) more than those in the control group.

However, there was no statistically significant difference in weight loss between the 8-hour and the 10-hour windows. The 8-hour window also showed no significant impact on blood pressure, glucose, or cholesterol.

“The findings are interesting and add to the evidence that shortening the daily eating window may help with weight loss, but I would be cautious about concluding that eight hours is the optimal window,” Dalia Perelman, MS, RDN, CDCES, research dietitian at Stanford Medicine, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

“One finding I find particularly interesting is that people who shortened their eating window more relative to their usual pattern tended to lose more weight. This suggests that the benefit may not be about everyone following exactly the same eight-hour window, but rather about meaningfully shortening one’s habitual eating period,” she added.

The researchers also found that the 10-hour eating window significantly reduced systolic blood pressure compared with the 12-hour window. There were no significant differences between the eating windows for glucose or lipids.

However, a 2020 study found that a 10-hour eating window reduced weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol, among adults with metabolic syndrome who were already taking medication.

“[These] effects are generally modest, and TRE should be viewed as one potential component of an overall lifestyle approach rather than a treatment on its own,” said Perelman.

“I think TRE is best viewed as one possible tool rather than a magic formula. When we eat appears to matter, but what and how much we eat still matter as well,” she added.

“A nutritious diet, limiting highly processed foods, avoiding eating late at night, and finding an eating pattern that is enjoyable and sustainable are probably more important than rigidly adhering to a specific number of hours.”

Perelman noted that TRE may not be right for everyone, including:

Perelman also told Healthline that “Older adults at risk for muscle loss should also make sure they are consuming adequate calories and protein.”

She added that people with diabetes who use insulin or medications that can cause hypoglycemia should discuss TRE with their healthcare professional because changing when they eat may require medication adjustments.

As with any eating plan, time-restricted eating should be realistic and sustainable for your lifestyle.

Perelman noted that health is about more than what and when you eat. She said that sharing meals with family and friends, social connection, and enjoyment of food are important too.

A rigid eating schedule that interferes with those things may not be beneficial overall.

“Rather than focusing on achieving a precise eight-hour window, I would prioritize a balanced, nutrient-rich diet low in highly processed foods and, when possible, finish eating earlier in the evening,” Perelman said.

#4826. The Patient Voice Was Invited Into the Room. Was It Heard?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Something has been bothering me since I spoke at a cardiology conference this summer.

The invitation felt significant. As both a psychologist and someone whose life has depended on cardiology since infancy, I was honoured to be part of a symposium alongside several highly respected professors. I arrived feeling optimistic.

For most of my life, congenital heart disease was viewed largely through a biomedical lens. Survival was the priority. While this has begun to change, I left the conference wondering how far we have really come.

Walking through the exhibition hall, I was struck by the advances in technology and clinical care. Yet as the day went on, I found myself thinking less about conditions and treatments and more about the people living through them.

One interaction stayed with me. Hoping to discuss patient experience, I approached a heart charity's stand. Staff appeared busy filming promotional content for social media. Perhaps I arrived at the wrong moment, but it felt symbolic: considerable attention devoted to communicating about patients, less directed toward listening to them.

The exhibition hall was unexpectedly triggering. Surrounded by equipment and technology, I was transported back to the hospitals of my childhood and had to step outside to ground myself. Yet these were not simply memories from a distant past. As someone who still lives with congenital heart disease and depends on ongoing specialist care, the world I was walking through was also part of my present and future.

Although I attended as a psychologist and researcher, I was also there as a patient. I have experienced recent setbacks in my cardiac health and am currently off work while trialling one of the medications discussed during the symposium.

The other presentations focused on highly technical aspects of cardiac care. I was discussing the psychological experience of living with congenital heart disease and a lifetime of medical intervention. I spent longer than usual on my own story because I wanted the audience to see healthcare through the eyes of a child receiving it.

As I spoke, several people left. They may have had other commitments, but the moment stayed with me because it echoed a question that had been growing throughout the day: What happens when discussion turns from disease to lived experience?

Later, I described childhood pacemaker checks: lying dizzy and breathless on a hospital bed while clinicians learned to use emerging technology, gripping my mother's hand and counting holes in ceiling tiles. A small ripple of laughter spread through the audience. I suspect people were responding to how much technology has changed. Yet I found myself wondering whether we had taken away the same story. I was describing what it felt like to be the child on the bed.

The final troubling moment came at the end of the session. Several speakers had overrun, and there was no time for questions after my presentation. Perhaps it was simply unfortunate timing, yet I could not ignore the symbolism. The one presentation focused on lived experience was the one that never became a conversation.

Perhaps part of what stayed with me was the contrast with psychology conferences, where lived experience often sits at the centre of discussion. These topics usually generate deep engagement and reflection. Their relative absence on this occasion left me wondering whether healthcare still finds it easier to engage with what can be measured and treated than with what it feels like to live through those experiences.

On the train home, I found myself thinking about the child I once was and the many children I had known on cardiac wards over the years—the ones lying in hospital beds while adults discussed conditions, procedures, and outcomes over their heads.

This is not a criticism of individual clinicians, many of whom are passionate advocates for psychologically informed care. Rather, it left me reflecting on a wider culture within healthcare. Even among deeply caring professionals, it can sometimes feel easier to discuss disease than lived experience.

I was also struck by how little attention was paid to the psychological well-being of healthcare professionals themselves. There was little discussion of burnout, compassion fatigue, vicarious trauma, or moral injury, despite these being well-recognised occupational risks.

Modern medicine has become remarkably effective at helping people survive. Understanding survival, however, is not the same as understanding what survival feels like.

The day also forced me to confront something I often overlook: the personal cost of repeatedly turning my own medical history into a teaching tool.

For years, I have shared my story in the hope of helping healthcare become more psychologically informed. Yet congenital heart disease is not a chapter of my life that ended in childhood. It is a lifelong condition that continues to shape my health, identity, and future. As someone who still depends on specialist cardiac care, I am never speaking solely about the past.

Looking after my own mental health is not separate from that work. It is what allows me to continue doing it.

As someone who has lived with congenital heart disease my entire life, I know how much has changed. When I was a child, survival was often the only conversation. Today, we know far more about the psychological realities of living with lifelong conditions and the importance of supporting patients, families, and healthcare professionals.

The evidence is there, yet psychologically informed care can still feel confined to a dedicated session or token talk rather than something embedded throughout healthcare. Patient experience should not be an optional addition to discussions of treatment and outcomes. It should help shape them.

Morton, L. (2026). Beyond the Medical Gaze: Practicing Psychologically Informed Healthcare. Oxford University Press.
